div2.head: [ACT I SCENE 1]

sp.speaker: WITGOOD
sp.p: All’s gone! Still thou’rt a gentleman, that’s all. But a poor one, that’s nothing. What milk brings thy meadows forth now? Where are thy goodly uplands and thy downlands? All sunk into that little pit, lechery. Why should a gallant pay but two shillings for his ord’nary that nourishes him, and twenty times two for his brothel that consumes him? But where’s Long-acre? In my uncle’s conscience, which is three years’ voyage about. He that sets out upon his conscience ne’er finds the way home again; he is either swallowed in the quicksands of law-quillets or splits upon the piles of a praemunire ; yet these old fox-brain’d and ox-brow’d uncles have still defences for their avarice and apologies for their practices, and will thus greet our follies:

lg.l: He that doth his youth expose
To brothel, drink, and danger,
Let him that is his nearest kin
Cheat him before a stranger.

sp.p: And that’s his uncle; ‘tis a principle in usury. I dare not visit the city; there I should be too soon visited by that horrible plague, my debts, and by that means I lose a virgin’s love, her portion, and her virtues. Well, how should a man live now that has no living? Hum. Why, are there not a million of men in the world that only sojourn upon their brain and make their wits their mercers? And am I but one amongst that million and cannot thrive upon’t? Any trick out of the compass of law now would come happily to me.

sp.speaker: COURTESAN
sp.p: My love!

sp.speaker: WITGOOD
sp.p: My loathing! Hast thou been the secret consumption of my purse, and now com’st to undo my last means, my wit? Wilt leave no virtue in me, and yet thou ne’er the better?

lg.l: Hence, courtesan, round-webb’d tarantula,
That dryest the roses in the cheeks of youth.
I have been true unto your pleasure, and all your lands
Thrice rack’d was never worth the jewel
Which I prodigally gave you, my virginity.
Lands mortgag’d may return, and more esteem’d,
But honesty once pawn’d is ne’er redeem’d.
Forgive; I do thee wrong
To make thee sin and then to chide thee for’t.
I know I am your loathing now; farewell.
Stay, best invention, stay.

sp.speaker: COURTESAN
sp.p: I that have been the secret consumption of your purse, shall I stay now to undo your last means, your wits? Hence, courtesan, away.

sp.speaker: WITGOOD
sp.p: I prithee make me not mad at my own weapon. Stay—a thing few women can do, I know that, and therefore they had need wear stays—be not contrary. Dost love me? Fate has so cast it that all my means I must derive from thee.

lg.l: From me? Be happy then;
What lies within the power of my performance
Shall be commanded of thee.
Spoke like
An honest drab, i’ faith; it may prove something.
What trick is not an embryo at first,
Until a perfect shape come over it?
Come, I must help you. Whereabouts left you?
I’ll proceed.
Though you beget, ‘tis I must help to breed.
Speak. What is’t? I’d fain conceive it.

sp.speaker: WITGOOD
sp.p: So, so, so. Thou shalt presently take the name and form upon thee of a rich country widow, four hundred a year valiant, in woods, in bullocks, in barns, and in rye stacks. We’ll to London and to my covetous uncle.

sp.speaker: COURTESAN
sp.p: I begin to applaud thee; our states being both desperate, they are soon resolute. But how for horses?

sp.speaker: WITGOOD
sp.p: Mass, that’s true. The jest will be of some continuance. Let me see. Horses now, a bots on ‘em! Stay. I have acquaintance with a mad host, never yet bawd to thee. I have rins’d the whoreson’s gums in mull-sack many a time and often; put but a good tale into his ear now so it come off cleanly, and there’s horse and man for us, I dare warrant thee.

lg.l: Arm your wits then
Speedily. There shall want nothing in me,
Either in behaviour, discourse, or fashion,
That shall discredit your intended purpose.
I will so artfully disguise my wants
And set so good a courage on my state
That I will be believed.

sp.speaker: WITGOOD
sp.p: Why, then, all’s furnish’d. I shall go nigh to catch that old fox mine uncle, though he make but some amends for my undoing. Yet there’s some comfort in’t: He cannot otherwise choose, though it be but in hope to cozen me again, but supply any hasty want that I bring to town with me. The device well and cunningly carried, the name of a rich widow and four hundred a year in good earth will so conjure up a kind of usurer’s love in him to me that he will not only desire my presence, which at first shall scarce be granted him—I’ll keep off a’ purpose— but I shall find him so officious to deserve, so ready to supply. I know the state of an old man’s affection so well: If his nephew be poor indeed, why he lets God alone with him, but if he be once rich, then he’ll be the first man that helps him.

sp.speaker: COURTESAN
sp.p: ‘Tis right the world; for in these days an old man’s love to his kindred is like his kindness to his wife, ‘tis always done before he comes at it.

sp.speaker: WITGOOD
sp.p: I owe thee for that jest. Begone. Here’s all my wealth. Prepare thyself. Away. I’ll to mine host with all possible haste, and, with the best art and most profitable form, pour the sweet circumstance into his ear, which shall have the gift to turn all the wax to honey. [Exit Courtesan] How now? Oh, the right worshipful seniors of our country.

div2.stage: [Enter Three Gentlemen Gentlemen Lawrence annotates: “Onesiphorus Hoard, Limber, and Kix, but not so identified until later (I,i,112: V,ii,44-64)” (p.11). ]

lg.l: Who’s that?
Oh, the common rioter. Take no note of him.

l.seg: You will not see me now; the comfort is
Ere it be long you will scarce see yourselves.

lg.l: I wonder how he breathes; h’as consum’d all
Upon that courtesan.
We have heard so much.
You have heard all truth; his uncle and my brother
Have been these three years mortal adversaries.
Two old tough spirits, they seldom meet but fight,
Or quarrel when ‘tis calmest. I think their anger
Be the very fire that keeps their age alive.

sp.speaker: 2 GENTLEMAN
sp.p: What was the quarrel, sir?

sp.speaker: 1 GENTLEMAN
sp.p: Faith, about a purchase, fetching over a young heir. Master Hoard, my brother, having wasted much time in beating the bargain, what did me old Lucre but, as his conscience mov’d him, knowing the poor gentleman, stepp’d in between ‘em and cozen’d him himself.

sp.speaker: 2 GENTLEMAN
sp.p: And was this all, sir?

sp.speaker: 1 GENTLEMAN
sp.p: This was e’en it, sir. Yet for all this, I know no reason but the match might go forward betwixt his wife’s son and my niece. What though there be a dissension between the two old men, I see no reason it should put a difference between the two younger. ‘Tis as natural for old folks to fall out as for young to fall in. A scholar comes a-wooing to my niece; well, he’s wise, but he’s poor. Her son comes a-wooing to my niece; well, he’s a fool, but he’s rich.

sp.speaker: 2 GENTLEMAN
sp.p: Ay, marry, sir.

sp.speaker: 1 GENTLEMAN
sp.p: Pray now, is not a rich fool better than a poor philosopher?

sp.speaker: 2 GENTLEMAN
sp.p: One would think so, i’ faith.

sp.speaker: 1 GENTLEMAN
sp.p: She now remains at London with my brother, her second uncle, to learn fashions, practise music. The voice between her lips, and the viol between her legs, she’ll be fit for a consort very speedily. A thousand good pound is her portion; if she marry, we’ll ride up and be merry.

sp.speaker: 3 GENTLEMAN
sp.p: A match, if it be a match.

div2.head: [ACT I SCENE 2]
div2.stage: Enter at one door, Witgood; at the other, Host

sp.speaker: WITGOOD
sp.p: Mine host?

sp.speaker: HOST
sp.p: Young Master Witgood.

sp.speaker: WITGOOD
sp.p: I have been laying all the town for thee.

sp.speaker: HOST
sp.p: Why, what’s the news, Bully Had-land?

sp.speaker: WITGOOD
sp.p: What geldings are in the house of thine own? Answer me to that first.

sp.speaker: HOST
sp.p: Why, man, why?

sp.speaker: WITGOOD
sp.p:
Mark me what I say. I’ll tell thee such a tale in thine ear that thou shalt trust me spite of thy teeth, furnish me with some money willy-nilly, and ride up with me thyself contra voluntatem
et professionem .

sp.speaker: HOST
sp.p: How! Let me see this trick, and I’ll say thou hast more art than a conjurer.

sp.speaker: WITGOOD
sp.p: Dost thou joy in my advancement?

sp.speaker: HOST
sp.p: Do I love sack and ginger?

sp.speaker: WITGOOD
sp.p: Comes my prosperity desiredly to thee?

sp.speaker: HOST
sp.p: Come forfeitures to a usurer, fees to an officer, punks to an host, and pigs to a parson desiredly? Why, then, la!

sp.speaker: WITGOOD
sp.p: Will the report of a widow of four hundred a year, boy, make thee leap and sing and dance and come to thy place again?

sp.speaker: HOST
sp.p: Wilt thou command me now? I am thy spirit; conjure me into any shape.

sp.speaker: WITGOOD
sp.p: I ha’ brought her from her friends, turn’d back the horses by a sleight. Not so much as one amongst her six men, goodly, large, yeomanly fellows, will she trust with this her purpose; by this light, all unmann’d; regardless of her state, neglectful of vainglorious ceremony, all for my love. Oh, ‘tis a fine little voluble tongue, mine host, that wins a widow.

sp.speaker: HOST
sp.p: No, ‘tis a tongue with a great T, my boy, that wins a widow.

sp.speaker: WITGOOD
sp.p: Now, sir, the case stands thus, good mine host; if thou lov’st my happiness, assist me.

sp.speaker: HOST
sp.p: Command all my beasts i’ th’ house.

sp.speaker: WITGOOD
sp.p: Nay, that’s not all neither; prithee, take truce with thy joy and listen to me. Thou know’st I have a wealthy uncle i’ th’ city, somewhat the wealthier by my follies. The report of this fortune, well and cunningly carried, might be a means to draw some goodness from the usuring rascal, for I have put her in hope already of some estate that I have, either in land or money. Now if I be found true in neither, what may I expect but a sudden breach of our love, utter dissolution of the match, and confusion of my fortunes for ever?

sp.speaker: HOST
sp.p: Wilt thou but trust the managing of thy business with me?

sp.speaker: WITGOOD
sp.p: With thee? Why, will I desire to thrive in my purpose? Will I hug four hundred a year? I that know the misery of nothing? Will that man wish a rich widow, that has ne’er a hole to put his head in? With thee, mine host? Why, believe it, sooner with thee than with a covey of counsellors.

sp.speaker: HOST
sp.p:
Thank you for your good report. I’ faith, sir, and if I stand you not in stead, why, then, let an host come off hic et haec
hostis , a deadly enemy to dice, drink, and venery. Come, where’s this widow?

sp.speaker: WITGOOD
sp.p: Hard at Park End.

sp.speaker: HOST
sp.p: I’ll be her serving-man for once.

sp.speaker: WITGOOD
sp.p: Why, there we let off together. Keep full time; my thoughts were striking then just the same number.

sp.speaker: HOST
sp.p: I knew’t. Shall we then see our merry days again?

sp.speaker: WITGOOD
sp.p: Our merry nights, which ne’er shall be more seen.

div2.head: [ACT I SCENE 3]
div2.stage: Enter at several doors old Lucre and old [Walkadine] Hoard, gentlemen [Lamprey, Spitchcock, Sam Freedom, and Moneylove] coming between them to pacify ‘em

sp.speaker: LAMPREY
sp.p: Nay, good Master Lucre, and you, Master Hoard, anger is the wind which you’re both too much troubled withal.

sp.speaker: WALKADINE HOARD
sp.p: Shall my adversary thus daily affront me, ripping up the old wound of our malice, which three summers could not close up? Into which wound the very sight of him drops scalding lead instead of balsamum?

sp.speaker: LUCRE
sp.p: Why, Hoard, Hoard, Hoard, Hoard, Hoard! May I not pass in the state of quietness to mine own house? Answer me to that, before witness, and why? I’ll refer the cause to honest, even-minded gentlemen, or require the mere indifferences of the law to decide this matter. I got the purchase, true; was’t not any man’s case? Yes. Will a wise man stand as a bawd, whilst another wipes his nose of the bargain? No, I answer, no, in that case.

sp.speaker: LAMPREY
sp.p: Nay, sweet Master Lucre.

sp.speaker: WALKADINE HOARD
sp.p: Was it the part of a friend? No; rather of a Jew. Mark what I say: When I had beaten the bush to the last bird, or, as I may term it, the price to a pound, then, like a cunning usurer, to come in the evening of the bargain and glean all my hopes in a minute; to enter, as it were, at the back door of the purchase, for thou ne’er cam’st the right way by it!

sp.speaker: LUCRE
sp.p: Hast thou the conscience to tell me so, without any impeachment to thyself?

sp.speaker: WALKADINE HOARD
sp.p: Thou that canst defeat thy own nephew, Lucre, lap his lands into bonds, and take the extremity of thy kindred’s forfeitures because he’s a rioter, a wastethrift, a brothel-master, and so forth—what may a stranger expect from thee but vulnera dilacerate , as the poet says, dilacerate dealing?

sp.speaker: LUCRE
sp.p: Upbraid’st thou me with ‘nephew’? Is all imputation laid upon me? What acquaintance have I with his follies? If he riot, ’tis he must want it; if he surfeit, ‘tis he must feel it; if he drab it, ‘tis he must lie by’t. What’s this to me?

sp.speaker: WALKADINE HOARD
sp.p: What’s all to thee? Nothing, nothing; such is the gulf of thy desire and the wolf of thy conscience. But be assured, old Pecunius Lucre, if ever fortune so bless me that I may be at leisure to vex thee, or any means so favour me that I may have opportunity to mad thee, I will pursue it with that flame of hate, that spirit of malice, unrepressed wrath, that I will blast thy comforts.

sp.speaker: LUCRE
sp.p: Ha, ha, ha!

sp.speaker: LAMPREY
sp.p: Nay, Master Hoard, you’re a wise gentleman.

sp.speaker: WALKADINE HOARD
sp.p: I will so cross thee—

sp.speaker: LUCRE
sp.p: And I thee.

sp.speaker: WALKADINE HOARD
sp.p: So without mercy fret thee—

sp.speaker: LUCRE
sp.p: So monstrously oppose thee—

sp.speaker: WALKADINE HOARD
sp.p: Dost scoff at my just anger? Oh, that I had as much power as usury has over thee!

sp.speaker: LUCRE
sp.p: Then thou wouldst have as much power as the devil has over thee!

sp.speaker: WALKADINE HOARD
sp.p: Toad!

sp.speaker: LUCRE
sp.p: Aspic!

sp.speaker: WALKADINE HOARD
sp.p: Serpent!

sp.speaker: LUCRE
sp.p: Viper!

sp.speaker: SPITCHCOCK
sp.p: Nay, gentlemen, then we must divide you perforce.

sp.speaker: LAMPREY
sp.p: When the fire grows too unreasonable hot, there’s no better way than to take off the wood.

div2.stage: Exeunt [Lamprey, Spitchcock, Lucre and Walkadine Hoard].

sp.speaker: SAM
sp.p: A word, good signior.

sp.speaker: MONEYLOVE
sp.p: How now, what’s the news?

sp.speaker: SAM
sp.p: ‘Tis given me to understand that you are a rival of mine in the love of Mistress Joyce, Master Hoard’s niece. Say me ay, say me no.

sp.speaker: MONEYLOVE
sp.p: Yes, ‘tis so.

sp.speaker: SAM
sp.p: Then look to yourself; you cannot live long. I’m practising every morning; a month hence I’ll challenge you.

sp.speaker: MONEYLOVE
sp.p: Give me your hand upon’t. There’s my pledge I’ll meet you!

sp.speaker: SAM
sp.p: Oh! Oh! What reason had you for that, sir, to strike before the month? You knew I was not ready for you, and that made you so crank. I am not such a coward to strike again, I warrant you; my ear has the law of her side, for it burns horribly. I will teach him to strike a naked face, the longest day of his life. ‘Slid, it shall cost me some money, but I’ll bring this box into the Chancery.

div2.head: [ACT I SCENE 4]

sp.speaker: HOST
sp.p: Fear you nothing, sir, I have lodg’d her in a house of credit, I warrant you.

sp.speaker: WITGOOD
sp.p: Hast thou the writings?

sp.speaker: HOST
sp.p: Firm, sir.

div2.stage: [Enter Dampit and Gulf, who stand apart]

sp.speaker: WITGOOD
sp.p: Prithee, stay, and behold two [of] the most prodigious rascals that ever slipp’d into the shape of men: Dampit, sirrah, and young Gulf, his fellow caterpillar.

sp.speaker: HOST
sp.p: Dampit? Sure, I have heard of that Dampit.

sp.speaker: WITGOOD.
sp.p: Heard of him? Why, man, he that has lost both his ears may hear of him; a famous infamous trampler of time (his own phrase). Note him well. That Dampit, sirrah, he in the uneven beard and the serge cloak, is the most notorious, usuring, blasphemous, atheistical, brothel-vomiting rascal that we have in these latter times now extant, whose first beginning was the stealing of a mastie dog from a farmer’s house.

sp.speaker: HOST
sp.p: He look’d as if he would obey the commandment[s] well, when he began first with stealing.

sp.speaker: WITGOOD
sp.p: True. The next town he came at, he set the dogs together by th’ears.

sp.speaker: HOST
sp.p: A sign he should follow the law, by my faith.

sp.speaker: WITGOOD
sp.p: So it followed, indeed; and being destitute of all fortunes, stak’d his mastie against a noble, and by great fortune his dog had the day. How he made it up ten shillings I know not, but his own boast is that he came to town with but ten shillings in his purse, and now is credibly worth ten thousand pound.

sp.speaker: HOST
sp.p: How the devil came he by it?

p.seg: A pox search you. The very loins of thee!

sp.speaker: GULF.
sp.p: He that walks low walks safe, the poets tell us.

p.seg: And nigher Hell by a foot and a half than the rest of his fellows

sp.speaker: DAMPIT
sp.p: My sweet Theodorus!

sp.speaker: WITGOOD
sp.p: ‘Twas a merry world when thou cam’st to town with ten shillings in thy purse.

sp.speaker: DAMPIT
sp.p: And now worth ten thousand pound, my boy. Report it: Harry Dampit, a trampler of time; say he would be up in a morning and be here with his serge gown, dash’d up to the hams in a cause, have his feet stink about Westminster Hall, and come home again; see the galleons, the galleasses, the great armadas of the law; then there be hoys and petty vessels, oars and scullers of the time; there be picklocks of the time too. Then would I be here; I would trample up and down like a mule; now to the judges: ‘May it please your reverend, honourable fatherhoods’; then to my counsellor: ‘May it please your worshipful patience’; then to the examiner’s office: ‘May it please your mastership’s gentleness’; then to one of the clerks: ‘May it please your worshipful lousiness’, for I find him scrubbing in his codpiece; then to the hall again; then to the chamber again—

sp.speaker: WITGOOD
sp.p: And when to the cellar again?

sp.speaker: DAMPIT
sp.p: E’en when thou wilt again. Tramplers of time, motions of Fleet Street, and visions of Holborn; here I have fees of one, there I have fees of another; my clients come about me, the fooliaminy and coxcombry of the country. I still trash’d and trotted for other men’s causes; thus was poor Harry Dampit made rich by others’ laziness, who, though they would not follow their own suits, I made ‘em follow me with their purses.

sp.speaker: WITGOOD
sp.p: Didst thou so, old Harry?

sp.speaker: DAMPIT
sp.p: Ay, and I sous’d ‘em with bills of charges, i’ faith; twenty pound a year have I brought in for boat-hire, and I ne’er stepp’d into boat in my life.

sp.speaker: WITGOOD
sp.p: Tramplers of time!

sp.speaker: DAMPIT
sp.p: Ay, tramplers of time, rascals of time, bull-beggars.

sp.speaker: WITGOOD
sp.p: Ah, thou’rt a mad old Harry! Kind Master Gulf, I am bold to renew my acquaintance.

sp.speaker: GULF.
sp.p: I embrace it, sir.

div2.head: <<Incipit>> ACT II [SCENE 1]

sp.speaker: LUCRE
sp.p: My adversary ever more twits me with my nephew; forsooth, my nephew, Why may not a virtuous uncle have a dissolute nephew? What though he be a brotheller, a waste-thrift, a common surfeiter, and, to conclude, a beggar? Must sin in him call up shame in me? Since we have no part in their follies, why should we have part in their infamies? For my strict hand towards his mortgage, that I deny not; I confess I had an uncle’s pen’worth. Let me see, half in half, true. I saw neither hope of his reclaiming nor comfort in his being, and was it not then better bestow’d upon his uncle than upon one of his aunts? I need not say ‘bawd’, for everyone knows what ‘aunt’ stands for in the last translation. [Enter Servant] Now, sir?

sp.speaker: SERVANT
sp.p: There’s a country serving-man, sir, attends to speak with your worship.

sp.speaker: LUCRE
sp.p: I’m at best leisure now; send him in to me.

sp.speaker: HOST
sp.p: Bless your venerable worship.

sp.speaker: LUCRE
sp.p: Welcome, good fellow.

p.seg: He calls me thief at first sight, yet he little thinks I am an host.

sp.speaker: LUCRE
sp.p: What’s thy business with me?

sp.speaker: HOST
sp.p: Faith, sir, I am sent from my mistress to any sufficient gentleman indeed, to ask advice upon a doubtful point. ‘Tis indifferent, sir, to whom I come, for I know none, nor did my mistress direct me to any particular man, for she’s as mere a stranger here as myself; only I found your worship within, and ‘tis a thing I ever lov’d, sir, to be dispatch’d as soon as I can.

p.seg: A good blunt honesty; I like him well.

sp.speaker: HOST
sp.p: Faith, a country gentlewoman, and a widow, sir. Yesterday was the first flight of us, but now she intends to stay until a little term business be ended.

sp.speaker: LUCRE
sp.p: Her name, I prithee.

sp.speaker: HOST
sp.p: It runs there in the writings, sir, among her lands, Widow Medlar.

sp.speaker: LUCRE
sp.p: Medlar? Mass, have I ne’er heard of that widow?

sp.speaker: HOST
sp.p: Yes, I warrant you, have you, sir; not the rich widow in Staffordshire?

sp.speaker: LUCRE
sp.p: Cuds me, there ‘tis, indeed. Thou hast put me into memory. There’s a widow indeed! Ah, that I were a bachelor again.

sp.speaker: HOST
sp.p: No doubt your worship might do much then, but she’s fairly promis’d to a bachelor already.

sp.speaker: LUCRE
sp.p: Ah, what is he, I prithee?

sp.speaker: HOST
sp.p: A country gentleman too, one whom your worship knows not, I’m sure; h’as spent some few follies in his youth, but marriage, by my faith, begins to call him home. My mistress loves him, sir, and love covers faults, you know. One Master Witgood, if ever you have heard of the gentleman.

sp.speaker: LUCRE
sp.p: Ha! Witgood, say’st thou?

sp.speaker: HOST
sp.p: That’s his name indeed, sir. My mistress is like to bring him to a goodly seat yonder; four hundred a year, by my faith.

sp.speaker: LUCRE
sp.p: But, I pray, take me with you.

sp.speaker: HOST
sp.p: Ay, sir.

sp.speaker: LUCRE
sp.p: What countryman might this young Witgood be?

sp.speaker: HOST
sp.p: A Leicestershire gentleman, sir.

p.seg: My nephew. By th’ mass, my nephew. I’ll fetch out more of this, i’ faith; a simple country fellow, I’ll work’t out of him.

sp.speaker: HOST
sp.p: Faith, he brought her up to town, sir; h’as the best card in all the bunch for’t, her heart; and I know my mistress will be married ere she go down. Nay, I’ll swear that, for she’s none of those widows that will go down first and be married after; she hates that, I can tell you, sir.

sp.speaker: LUCRE
sp.p: By my faith, sir, she is like to have a proper gentleman and a comely; I’ll give her that gift.

sp.speaker: HOST
sp.p: Why, does your worship know him, sir?

sp.speaker: LUCRE
sp.p: I know him? Does not all the world know him? Can a man of such exquisite qualities be hid under a bushel?

sp.speaker: HOST
sp.p: Then your worship may save me a labour, for I had charge given me to inquire after him.

sp.speaker: LUCRE
sp.p: Inquire of him? If I might counsel thee, thou shouldst ne’er trouble thyself further. Inquire of him of no more but of me; I’ll fit thee. I grant he has been youthful, but is he not now reclaim’d? Mark you that, sir. Has not your mistress, think you, been wanton in her youth? If men be wags, are there not women wagtails?

sp.speaker: HOST
sp.p: No doubt, sir.

sp.speaker: LUCRE
sp.p: Does not he return wisest that comes home whipp’d with his own follies?

sp.speaker: HOST
sp.p: Why, very true, sir.

sp.speaker: LUCRE
sp.p: The worst report you can hear of him, I can tell you, is that he has been a kind gentleman, a liberal, and a worthy; who but lusty Witgood, thrice-noble Witgood?

sp.speaker: HOST
sp.p: Since your worship has so much knowledge in him, can you resolve me, sir, what his living might be? My duty binds me, sir, to have a care of my mistress’ estate. She has been ever a good mistress to me, though I say it. Many wealthy suitors has she nonsuited for his sake; yet, though her love be so fix’d, a man cannot tell whether his nonperformance may help to remove it, sir. He makes us believe he has lands and living.

sp.speaker: LUCRE
sp.p: Who? Young Master Witgood? Why believe it, he has as goodly a fine living out yonder—what do you call the place?

sp.speaker: HOST
sp.p: Nay, I know not, i’ faith.

sp.speaker: LUCRE
sp.p: Hum. See like a beast, if I have not forgot the name. Pooh! And out yonder again, goodly grown woods and fair meadows—Pax on’t, I can ne’er hit of that place neither. He? Why, he’s Witgood of Witgood Hall; he, an unknown thing?

sp.speaker: HOST
sp.p: Is he so, sir? To see how rumour will alter! Trust me, sir, we heard once he had no lands, but all lay mortgag’d to an uncle he has in town here.

sp.speaker: LUCRE
sp.p: Push! ‘Tis a tale, ‘tis a tale.

sp.speaker: HOST
sp.p: I can assure you, sir, ‘twas credibly reported to my mistress.

sp.speaker: LUCRE
sp.p: Why, do you think, i’ faith, he was ever so simple to mortgage his lands to his uncle, or his uncle so unnatural to take the extremity of such a mortgage?

sp.speaker: HOST
sp.p: That was my saying still, sir.

sp.speaker: LUCRE
sp.p: Pooh! Ne’er think it.

sp.speaker: HOST
sp.p: Yet that report goes current.

lg.l: Nay, then, you urge me.
Cannot I tell that best that am his uncle.

sp.speaker: HOST
sp.p: How, sir! What have I done?

sp.speaker: LUCRE
sp.p: Why, how now? In a sound, man?

sp.speaker: HOST
sp.p: Is your worship his uncle, sir?

sp.speaker: LUCRE
sp.p: Can that be any harm to you, sir?

sp.speaker: HOST
sp.p: I do beseech you, sir, do me the favour to conceal it. What a beast was I to utter so much! Pray, sir, do me the kindness to keep it in. I shall have my coat pull’d o’er my ears an’t should be known; for the truth is, an’t please your worship, to prevent much rumour and many suitors, they intend to be married very suddenly and privately.

sp.speaker: LUCRE
sp.p: And dost thou think it stands with my judgment to do them injury? Must I needs say the knowledge of this marriage comes from thee? Am I a fool at fifty-four? Do I lack subtlety now, that have got all my wealth by it? There’s a leash of angels for thee. Come, let me woo thee. Speak. Where lie they?

sp.speaker: HOST
sp.p: So I might have no anger, sir,—

sp.speaker: LUCRE
sp.p: Passion of me, not a jot. Prithee, come.

sp.speaker: HOST
sp.p: I would not have it known it came by my means.

sp.speaker: LUCRE
sp.p: Why, am I a man of wisdom?

sp.speaker: HOST
sp.p: I dare trust your worship, sir, but I’m a stranger to your house, and to avoid all intelligencers I desire your worship’s ear.

p.seg: This fellow’s worth a matter of trust. Ah, sirrah nephew!

sp.speaker: HOST
sp.p: Please you, sir, now I have begun with your worship, when shall I attend for your advice upon that doubtful point? I must come warily now.

lg.l: Tut, fear thou nothing.
Tomorrow’s evening shall resolve the doubt.

sp.speaker: HOST
sp.p: The time shall cause my attendance.

sp.speaker: LUCRE
sp.p: Fare thee well. There’s more true honesty in such a country serving-man than in a hundred of our cloak companions. I may well call ‘em companions, for since blue coats have been turn’d into cloaks, we can scarce know the man from the master. George!

sp.speaker: GEORGE
sp.p: Anon, sir.

sp.speaker: LUCRE
sp.p: List hither. [Whispers] Keep the place secret. Commend me to my nephew. I know no cause, tell him, but he might see his uncle.

sp.speaker: GEORGE
sp.p: I will, sir.

lg.l: And, do you hear, sir?
Take heed you use him with respect and duty.

p.seg: Here’s a strange alteration. One day he must be turn’d out like a beggar, and now he must be call’d in like a knight.

sp.speaker: LUCRE
sp.p: Ah, sirrah, that rich widow! Four hundred a year! Beside, I hear she lays claim to a title of a hundred more. This falls unhappily that he should bear a grudge to me now, being likely to prove so rich. What is’t, trow, that he makes me a stranger for? Hum, I hope he has not so much wit to apprehend that I cozened him; he deceives me then. Good Heaven, who would have thought it would ever have come to this pass? Yet he’s a proper gentleman, i’ faith, give him his due. Marry, that’s his mortgage, but that I ne’er mean to give him. I’ll make him rich enough in words, if that be good; and if it come to a piece of money, I will not greatly stick for’t. There may be hope some of the widow’s lands too may one day fall upon me, if things be carried wisely. [Enter George] Now, sir, where is he?

sp.speaker: GEORGE
sp.p: He desires your worship to hold him excused; he has such weighty business it commands him wholly from all men.

sp.speaker: LUCRE
sp.p: Were those my nephew’s words?

sp.speaker: GEORGE
sp.p: Yes, indeed, sir.

p.seg: When men grow rich they grow proud too, I perceive that. He would not have sent me such an answer once within this twelvemonth; see what ‘tis when a man’s come to his lands.
This is good sport, i’ faith.

sp.speaker: LUCRE
sp.p: Troth, he uses his uncle discourteously now. Can he tell what I may do for him? Goodness may come from me in a minute that comes not in seven year again. He knows my humour; I am not so usually good. ‘Tis no small thing that draws kindness from me; he may know that, and he will. The chief cause that invites me to do him most good is the sudden astonishing of old Hoard, my adversary. How pale his malice will look at my nephew’s advancement! With what a dejected spirit he will behold his fortunes, whom but last day he proclaimed rioter, penurious makeshift, despised brothel-master! Ha, ha! ‘Twill do me more secret joy than my last purchase, more precious comfort than all these widows’ revenues.— Enter [George and] and Witgood Now, sir.

sp.speaker: GEORGE
sp.p: With much entreaty he’s at length come, sir.

sp.speaker: LUCRE
sp.p: Oh, nephew, let me salute you, sir; you’re welcome, nephew.

sp.speaker: WITGOOD
sp.p: Uncle, I thank you.

sp.speaker: LUCRE
sp.p: Y’ave a fault, nephew: You’re a stranger here. Well, Heaven give you joy!

sp.speaker: WITGOOD
sp.p: Of what, sir?

lg.l: Ha, we can hear.
You might have known your uncle’s house, i’ faith,
You and your widow. Go to, you were to blame,
If I may tell you so without offence.
How could you hear of that, sir?
Oh, pardon me!
It was your will to have it kept from me, I perceive now.

sp.speaker: WITGOOD
sp.p: Not for any defect of love, I protest, uncle.

sp.speaker: LUCRE
sp.p: Oh, ‘twas unkindness, nephew. Fie, fie, fie!

sp.speaker: WITGOOD
sp.p: I am sorry you take it in that sense, sir.

sp.speaker: LUCRE
sp.p: Pooh! You cannot colour it, i’ faith, nephew.

sp.speaker: WITGOOD
sp.p: Will you but hear what I can say in my just excuse, sir?

sp.speaker: LUCRE
sp.p: Yes, faith, will I, and welcome.

sp.speaker: WITGOOD
sp.p: You that know my danger i’ th’ city, sir, so well, how great my debts are, and how extreme my creditors, could not out of your pure judgment, sir, have wish’d us hither.

sp.speaker: LUCRE
sp.p: Mass, a firm reason indeed.

sp.speaker: WITGOOD
sp.p: Else my uncle’s house, why, ‘t ‘ad been the only make-match—

sp.speaker: LUCRE
sp.p: Nay, and thy credit.

sp.speaker: WITGOOD
sp.p: My credit? Nay, my countenance! Push! Nay, I know, uncle, you would have wrought it so. By your wit you would have made her believe in time the whole house had been mine—

sp.speaker: LUCRE
sp.p: Ay, and most of the goods too.

sp.speaker: WITGOOD
sp.p: La, you there. Well, let ‘em all prate what they will, there’s nothing like the bringing of a widow to one’s uncle’s house.

sp.speaker: LUCRE
sp.p: Nay, let nephews be ruled as they list, they shall find their uncle’s house the most natural place when all’s done.

sp.speaker: WITGOOD
sp.p: There they may be bold.

sp.speaker: LUCRE
sp.p: Life, they may do anything there, man, and fear neither beadle nor sum’ner. An uncle’s house, a very Cole Harbour! Sirrah, I’ll touch thee near now. Hast thou so much interest in thy widow that by a token thou couldst presently send for her?

sp.speaker: WITGOOD
sp.p: Troth, I think I can, uncle.

sp.speaker: LUCRE
sp.p: Go to, let me see that.

sp.speaker: WITGOOD
sp.p: Pray, command one of your men hither, uncle.

sp.speaker: LUCRE
sp.p: George!

sp.speaker: GEORGE
sp.p: Here, sir.

p.seg: I love a’ life to prattle with a rich widow; ‘tis pretty, methinks, when our tongues go together, and then to promise much and perform little. I love that sport a’ life, i’ faith, yet I am in the mood now to do my nephew some good, if he take me handsomely.

sp.speaker: WITGOOD
sp.p: I ha’ sent, sir.

sp.speaker: LUCRE
sp.p: Yet I must condemn you of unkindness, nephew.

sp.speaker: WITGOOD
sp.p: Heaven forbid, uncle!

sp.speaker: LUCRE
sp.p: Yes, faith, must I. Say your debts be many, your creditors importunate, yet the kindness of a thing is all, nephew; you might have sent me close word on’t, without the least danger or prejudice to your fortunes.

sp.speaker: WITGOOD
sp.p: Troth, I confess it, uncle; I was too blame there, but indeed my intent was to have clapp’d it up suddenly, and so have broke forth like a joy to my friends and a wonder to the world. Beside, there’s a trifle of a forty-pound matter towards the setting of me forth. My friends should ne’er have known on’t; I meant to make shift for that myself.

sp.speaker: LUCRE
sp.p: How, nephew! Let me not hear such a word again, I beseech you. Shall I be beholding to you?

sp.speaker: WITGOOD
sp.p: To me? Alas, what do you mean, uncle?

sp.speaker: LUCRE
sp.p: I charge you, upon my love. You trouble nobody but myself.

sp.speaker: WITGOOD.
sp.p: Y’ave no reason for that, uncle.

sp.speaker: LUCRE
sp.p: Troth, I’ll ne’er be friends with you while you live and you do.

sp.speaker: WITGOOD
sp.p: Nay, and you say so, uncle. Here’s my hand; I will not do’t—

sp.speaker: LUCRE
sp.p: Why, well said. There’s some hope in thee when thou wilt be ruled. I’ll make it up fifty, faith, because I see thee so reclaimed. Peace, here comes my wife with Sam, her tother husband’s son.

sp.speaker: WITGOOD
sp.p: Good aunt,—

sp.speaker: SAM
sp.p: Cousin Witgood! I rejoice in my salute; you’re most welcome to this noble city, govern’d with the sword in the scabbard.

p.seg: And the wit in the pommel!

sp.speaker: LUCRE
sp.p: By the mass, she’s coming, wife; let me see now how thou wilt entertain her.

sp.speaker: WIFE
sp.p: I hope I am not to learn, sir, to entertain a widow; ‘tis not so long ago since I was one myself.

sp.speaker: WITGOOD
sp.p: Uncle,—

sp.speaker: LUCRE
sp.p: She’s come indeed.

sp.speaker: WITGOOD
sp.p: My uncle was desirous to see you, widow, and I presum’d to invite you.

sp.speaker: COURTESAN
sp.p: The presumption was nothing. Master Witgood. Is this your uncle, sir?

sp.speaker: LUCRE
sp.p: Marry am I, sweet widow, and his good uncle he shall find me. Ay, by this smack that I give thee, thou’rt welcome. Wife, bid the widow welcome the same way again.

p.seg: I am a gentleman now too, by my father’s occupation, and I see no reason but I may kiss a widow by my father’s copy. Truly, I think the charter is not against it; surely these are the words: ‘The son, once a gentleman, may revel it, though his father were a dauber’. ‘Tis about the fifteenth page. I’ll to her.

div2.stage: [Attempts to kiss the Courtesan and is repulsed]

sp.speaker: LUCRE
sp.p: Y’are not very busy now; a word with thee, sweet widow.

p.seg: Coad’s nigs! I was never so disgrac’d since the hour my mother whipp’d me!

sp.speaker: LUCRE
sp.p: Beside, I have no child of mine own to care for; she’s my second wife, old, past bearing. Clap sure to him, widow; he’s like to be my heir, I can tell you.

sp.speaker: COURTESAN
sp.p: Is he so, sir?

sp.speaker: LUCRE
sp.p: He knows it already, and the knave’s proud on’t. Jolly rich widows have been offer’d him here i’ th’ city, great merchants’ wives, and do you think he would once look upon ‘em? Forsooth, he’ll none. You are beholding to him i’ th’ country then, ere we could be; nay, I’ll hold a wager, widow, if he were once known to be in town, he would be presently sought after; nay, and happy were they that could catch him first.

sp.speaker: COURTESAN
sp.p: I think so.

sp.speaker: LUCRE
sp.p: Oh, there would be such running to and fro, widow, he should not pass the streets for ‘em; he’d be took up in one great house or other presently. Faugh, they know he has it and must have it. You see this house here, widow? This house and all comes to him! Goodly rooms ready furnish’d, ceil’d with plaster of Paris, and all hung about with cloth of arras. Nephew!

sp.speaker: WITGOOD
sp.p: Sir?

p.seg: Nephew, strike all sure above and thou be’st a good boy. Ah,

sp.speaker: WITGOOD
sp.p: Alas, sir, I know not how she would take it.

p.seg: So, let ‘em agree as they will now. Many a match has been struck up in my house i’ this fashion. Let ’em try all manner of ways, still there’s nothing like an uncle’s house to strike the stroke in. I’ll hold my wife in talk a little.

sp.speaker: WIFE
sp.p: Well, we must do as we may, sir.

sp.speaker: LUCRE
sp.p: I’ll have his money ready told for him again he come down. Let me see too. By th’ mass, I must present the widow with some jewel, a good piece of plate, or such a device; ‘twill hearten her on well. I have a very fair standing cup, and a good high standing cup will please a widow above all other pieces.

sp.speaker: WIFE
sp.p: Do you mock us with your nephew? I have a plot in my head, son; i’ faith, husband, to cross you.

sp.speaker: SAM
sp.p: Is it a tragedy plot or a comedy plot, good mother?

sp.speaker: WIFE
sp.p: ‘Tis a plot shall vex him. I charge you, of my blessing, son Sam, that you presently withdraw the action of your love from Master Hoard’s niece.

sp.speaker: SAM
sp.p: How, mother!

sp.speaker: WIFE
sp.p: Nay, I have a plot in my head, i’ faith. Here, take this chain of gold and this fair diamond. Dog me the widow home to her lodging, and at thy best opportunity fasten ‘em both upon her. Nay, I have a reach I can tell you. Thou art known what thou art, son, among the right worshipful, all the twelve companies.

sp.speaker: SAM
sp.p: Truly, I thank ‘em for it.

sp.speaker: WIFE
sp.p: He? He’s a scab to thee! And so certify her thou hast two hundred a year of thyself, besides thy good parts, a proper person and a lovely. If I were a widow I could find it in my heart to have thee myself, son, ay, from ‘em all.

sp.speaker: SAM
sp.p: Thank you for your good will, mother, but indeed I had rather have a stranger. And if I woo her not in that violent fashion, that I will make her be glad to take these gifts ere I leave her, let me never be called the heir of your body.

sp.speaker: WIFE
sp.p: Nay, I know there’s enough in you, son, if you once come to put it forth.

sp.speaker: SAM
sp.p: I’ll quickly make a bolt or a shaft on’t.

sp.speaker: MONEYLOVE
sp.p: Faith, Master Hoard, I have bestowed many months in the suit of your niece, such was the dear love I ever bore to her virtues, but since she hath so extremely denied me, I am to lay out for my fortunes elsewhere.

sp.speaker: WALKADINE HOARD
sp.p: Heaven forbid but you should, sir; I ever told you my niece stood otherwise affected.

sp.speaker: MONEYLOVE
sp.p: I must confess you did, sir; yet in regard of my great loss of time and the zeal with which I sought your niece, shall I desire one favour of your worship?

sp.speaker: WALKADINE HOARD
sp.p: In regard of those two, ‘tis hard, but you shall, sir.

sp.speaker: MONEYLOVE
sp.p: I shall rest grateful. ‘Tis not full three hours, sir, since the happy rumour of a rich country widow came to my hearing.

sp.speaker: WALKADINE HOARD
sp.p: How! A rich country widow?

sp.speaker: MONEYLOVE
sp.p: Four hundred a year, landed.

sp.speaker: WALKADINE HOARD
sp.p: Yea?

sp.speaker: MONEYLOVE
sp.p: Most firm, sir, and I have learn’d her lodging. Here my suit begins, sir: If I might but entreat your worship to be a countenance for me and speak a good word—for your words will pass—I nothing doubt but I might set fair for the widow; nor shall your labour, sir, end altogether in thanks—two hundred angels—

sp.speaker: WALKADINE HOARD
sp.p: So, so. What suitors has she?

sp.speaker: MONEYLOVE
sp.p: There lies the comfort, sir; the report of her is yet but a whisper, and only solicited by young riotous Witgood, nephew to your mortal adversary.

sp.speaker: WALKADINE HOARD
sp.p: Ha! Art certain he’s her suitor?

sp.speaker: MONEYLOVE
sp.p: Most certain, sir, and his uncle very industrious to beguile the widow and make up the match.

p.seg: So! Very good.

sp.speaker: MONEYLOVE
sp.p: Now, sir, you know this young Witgood is a spendthrift, dissolute fellow.

sp.speaker: WALKADINE HOARD
sp.p: A very rascal.

sp.speaker: MONEYLOVE
sp.p: A midnight surfeiter.

sp.speaker: WALKADINE HOARD
sp.p: The spume of a brothel-house.

sp.speaker: MONEYLOVE
sp.p: True, sir; which being well told in your worship’s phrase may both heave him out of her mind, and drive a fair way for me to the widow’s affections.

sp.speaker: WALKADINE HOARD
sp.p: Attend me about five.

sp.speaker: MONEYLOVE
sp.p: With my best care, sir.

sp.speaker: WALKADINE HOARD

lg.l: Fool, thou hast left thy treasure with a thief,
To trust a widower with a suit in love!

sp.p: Happy revenge, I hug thee. I have not only the means laid before me extremely to cross my adversary and confound the last hopes of his nephew, but thereby to enrich my state, augment my revenues, and build mine own fortunes greater. Ha, ha!

lg.l: I’ll mar your phrase, o’erturn your flatteries,
Undo your windings, policies, and plots,
Fall like a secret and dispatchful plague
On your secured comforts. Why, I am able
To buy three of Lucre, thrice outbid him,
Let my out-monies be reckon’d and all.

sp.speaker: 1 CREDITOR
sp.p: I am glad of this news.

sp.speaker: 2 CREDITOR
sp.p: So are we, by my faith.

sp.speaker: 3 CREDITOR
sp.p: Young Witgood will be a gallant again now.

p.seg: Peace!

sp.speaker: 1 CREDITOR
sp.p: I promise you, Master Cockpit, she’s a mighty rich widow.

sp.speaker: 2 CREDITOR
sp.p: Why, have you ever heard of her?

sp.speaker: 1 CREDITOR
sp.p: Who, widow Medlar? She lies open to much rumour.

sp.speaker: 3 CREDITOR
sp.p: Four hundred a year, they say, in very good land.

sp.speaker: 1 CREDITOR
sp.p: Nay, tak't of my word, if you believe that, you believe the least.

sp.speaker: 2 CREDITOR
sp.p: And to see how close he keeps it!

sp.speaker: 1 CREDITOR
sp.p: Oh, sir, there’s policy in that, to prevent better suitors.

sp.speaker: 3 CREDITOR
sp.p: He owes me a hundred pound, and I protest I ne’er look’d for a penny.

sp.speaker: 1 CREDITOR
sp.p: He little dreams of our coming; he’ll wonder to see his creditors upon him.

lg.l: Good, his creditors. I’ll follow. This makes for me.
All know the widow’s wealth, and ‘tis well known
I can estate her fairly, ay, and will.
In this one chance shines a twice-happy fate;
I both deject my foe and raise my state.

sp.speaker: WITGOOD
sp.p: Why, alas, my creditors, could you find no other time to undo me but now? Rather your malice appears in this than the justness of the debt.

sp.speaker: 1 CREDITOR
sp.p: Master Witgood, I have forborne my money long.

sp.speaker: WITGOOD
sp.p: I pray, speak low, sir. What do you mean?

sp.speaker: 2 CREDITOR
sp.p: We hear you are to married suddenly to a rich country widow.

sp.speaker: WITGOOD
sp.p: What can be kept so close but you creditors hear on’t? Well, ‘tis a lamentable state that our chiefest afflicters should first hear of our fortunes. Why, this is no good course, i’ faith, sirs. If ever you have hope to be satisfied, why do you seek to confound the means that should work it? There’s neither piety, no, nor policy in that. Shine favourably now, why I may rise and spread again, to your great comforts.

sp.speaker: 1 CREDITOR
sp.p: He says true, i’ faith.

sp.speaker: WITGOOD
sp.p: Remove me now, and I consume for ever.

sp.speaker: 2 CREDITOR
sp.p: Sweet gentleman!

sp.speaker: WITGOOD
sp.p: How can it thrive which from the sun you sever?

sp.speaker: 3 CREDITOR
sp.p: It cannot indeed.

lg.l: Oh, then, show patience; I shall have enough
To satisfy you all.
Ay, if we could
Be content, a shame take us.
For, look you,
I am but newly sure yet to the widow,
And what a rend might this discredit make!
Within these three days will I bind you lands
For your securities.
No, good Master Witgood;
Would ‘twere as much as we dare trust you with.
I know you have been kind; however, now
Either by wrong report or false incitement,
Your gentleness is injur’d; in such
A state as this a man cannot want foes.
If on the sudden he begin to rise,
No man that lives can count his enemies.
You had some intelligence, I warrant ye,
From an ill-willer.

sp.speaker: 2 CREDITOR
sp.p: Faith, we heard you brought up a rich widow, sir, and were suddenly to marry her.

sp.speaker: WITGOOD
sp.p: Ay. Why, there it was; I knew ‘twas so. But since you are so well resolv’d of my faith toward you, let me be so much favour’d of you, I beseech you all—

sp.speaker: ALL
sp.p: Oh, it shall not need, i’ faith, sir,—

sp.speaker: WITGOOD
sp.p: As to lie still awhile and bury my debts in silence, till I be fully possess’d of the widow. For the truth is, I may tell you as my friends—

sp.speaker: ALL
sp.p: Oh, oh, oh!

sp.speaker: WITGOOD
sp.p: I am to raise a little money in the city toward the setting forth of myself, for mine own credit and your comfort. Now if my former debts should be divulg’d, all hope of my proceedings were quite extinguish’d.

sp.speaker: 1 CREDITOR
sp.p: [To Witgood] Do you hear, sir? I may deserve your custom hereafter. Pray, let my money be accepted before a stranger’s. Here’s forty pound I receiv’d as I came to you; if that may stand you in any stead, make use on’t. Nay, pray, sir, ‘tis at your service.

sp.speaker: WITGOOD
sp.p: [To 1 Creditor] You do so ravish me with kindness that I’m constrain’d to play the maid and take it.

sp.speaker: 1 CREDITOR
sp.p: [To Witgood] Let none of them see it, I beseech you.

p.seg: Faugh!

lg.l: [To Witgood] I hope I shall be first in your remembrance
After the marriage rites.

sp.speaker: WITGOOD
sp.p: [To 1 Creditor] Believe it firmly.

sp.speaker: 1 CREDITOR
sp.p: So.—What, do you walk, sirs?

sp.speaker: 2 CREDITOR
sp.p: I go. [To Witgood] Take no care, sir, for money to furnish you. Within this hour I’ll send you sufficient.—Come, Master Cockpit, we both stay for you.

sp.speaker: 3 CREDITOR
sp.p: I ha’ lost a ring, i’ faith; I’ll follow you presently. [Exeunt 1 and 2 Creditors] But you shall find it, sir. I know your youth and expenses have disfunish’d you of all jewels. There’s a ruby of twenty pound price, sir; bestow it upon your widow. What, man! ‘Twill call up her blood to you. Beside, if I might so much work with you, I would not have you beholding to those blood-suckers for any money.

sp.speaker: WITGOOD
sp.p: Not I, believe it.

sp.speaker: 3 CREDITOR
sp.p: Th’are a brace of cutthroats.

sp.speaker: WITGOOD
sp.p: I know ‘em.

sp.speaker: 3 CREDITOR
sp.p: Send a note of all your wants to my shop, and I’ll supply you instantly.

sp.speaker: WITGOOD
sp.p: Say you so? Why, here’s my hand then; no man living shall do’t but thyself.

sp.speaker: 3 CREDITOR
sp.p: Shall I carry it away from ‘em both then?

sp.speaker: WITGOOD
sp.p: I’ faith, shalt thou.

sp.speaker: 3 CREDITOR
sp.p: Troth, then, I thank you, sir.

sp.speaker: WITGOOD
sp.p: Welcome, good Master Cockpit. Exit [3 Creditor] Ha, ha, ha! Why, is not this better now than lying abed? I perceive there’s nothing conjures up wit sooner than poverty, and nothing lays it down sooner than wealth and lechery. This has some savour yet. Oh that I had the mortgage from mine uncle as sure in possession as these trifles, I would forswear brothel at noonday and muscadine and eggs at midnight!

sp.speaker: COURTESAN
sp.p: Master Witgood, where are you?

sp.speaker: WITGOOD
sp.p: Holla!

sp.speaker: COURTESAN
sp.p: Rich news!

sp.speaker: WITGOOD
sp.p: Would ‘twere all in plate!

sp.speaker: COURTESAN
sp.p: There’s some in chains and jewels. I am so haunted with suitors, Master Witgood, I know not which to dispatch first.

sp.speaker: WITGOOD
sp.p: You have the better term, by my faith!

lg.l: Among the number,
One Master Hoard, an ancient gentleman.

sp.speaker: WITGOOD
sp.p: Upon my life, my uncle’s adversary!

lg.l: It may well hold so, for he rails on you,
Speaks shamefully of him.
As I could wish it.
I first denied him, but so cunningly
It rather promis’d him assured hopes
Than any loss of labour.
Excellent.
I expect him every hour, with gentlemen
With whom he labours to make good his words,
To approve you riotous, your state consum’d,
Your uncle—

sp.speaker: WITGOOD
sp.p: Wench, make up thy own fortunes now; do thyself a good turn once in thy days. He’s rich in money, movables, and lands. Marry him. He’s an old doting fool, and that’s worth all. Marry him. ‘Twould be a great comfort to me to see thee do well, i’ faith. Marry him. ‘Twould ease my conscience well to see thee well bestow’d. I have a care of thee, i’ faith.

sp.speaker: COURTESAN
sp.p: Thanks, sweet Master Witgood.

sp.speaker: WITGOOD
sp.p: I reach at farther happiness. First, I am sure it can be no harm to thee, and there may happen goodness to me by it. Prosecute it well. Let’s send up for our wits, now we require their best and most pregnant assistance.

sp.speaker: COURTESAN
sp.p: Step in. I think I hear ‘em.

div2.head: [ACT III SCENE 2]
div2.stage: Enter [Walkadine] Hoard and Gentlemen, Gentlemen, Lawrence annotates “Perhaps Lamprey and Spitchcock” (p. 34) with the Host [as] serving-man

sp.speaker: WALKADINE HOARD
sp.p: Art thou the widow’s man? By my faith, sh’as a company of proper men then.

sp.speaker: HOST
sp.p: I am the worst of six, sir, good enough for blue coats.

sp.speaker: WALKADINE HOARD
sp.p: Hark hither. I hear say thou art in most credit with her.

sp.speaker: HOST
sp.p: Not so, sir.

sp.speaker: WALKADINE HOARD
sp.p: Come, come, thou’rt modest. There’s a brace of royals; prithee, help me to th’ speech of her.

sp.speaker: HOST
sp.p: I’ll do what I may, sir, always saving myself harmless.

sp.speaker: WALKADINE HOARD
sp.p: Go to. Do’t, I say. Thou shalt hear better from me.

p.seg: Is not this a better place than five mark a year standing wages? Say a man had but three such clients in a day, methinks he might make a poor living on’t. Beside, I was never brought up with so little honesty to refuse any man’s money. Never! What gulls there are a’ this side the world! Now know I the widow’s mind, none but my young master comes in her clutches. Ha, ha, ha!

lg.l: Now, my dear gentlemen, stand firmly to me.
You know his follies and my worth.
We do, sir.

sp.speaker: 2 GENTLEMAN
sp.p: But, Master Hoard, are you sure he is not i’ th’ house now?

lg.l: Upon my honesty, I chose this time
A’ purpose, fit. The spendthrift is abroad.
Assist me; here she comes.
Now, my sweet widow.
Y’are welcome, Master Hoard.
[To Gentlemen] Dispatch, sweet gentlemen, dispatch.—
I am come, widow, to prove those my words
Neither of envy sprung nor of false tongues,
But such as their deserts and actions
Do merit and bring forth; all which these gentlemen,
Well known and better reputed, will confess.
I cannot tell
How my affections may dispose of me,
But surely if they find him so desertless
They’ll have that reason to withdraw themselves.
And therefore, gentlemen, I do entreat you,
As you are fair in reputation,
And in appearing form, so shine in truth.
I am a widow, and, alas, you know
Soon overthrown; ‘tis a very small thing
That we withstand, our weakness is so great.
Be partial unto neither, but deliver,
Without affection, your opinion.
And that will drive it home.
Nay, I beseech your silence, Master Hoard;
You are a party.
Widow, not a word!
The better first to work you to belief,
Know neither of us owe him flattery,
Nor tother malice, but unbribed censure,
So help us our best fortunes.
It suffices.
That Witgood is a riotous, undone man,
Imperfect both in fame and in estate,
His debts wealthier than he, and executions
In wait for his due body, we’ll maintain
With our best credit and our dearest blood.
Nor land nor living, say you? Pray, take heed
You do not wrong the gentleman.
What we speak
Our lives and means are ready to make good.
Alas, how soon are we poor souls beguil’d!
And for his uncle,—
Let that come to me.
His uncle, a severe extortioner,
A tyrant at a forfeiture, greedy of others’
Miseries, one that would undo his brother,
Nay, swallow up his father if he can,
Within the fathoms of his conscience.
Nay, believe it, widow,
You had not only match’d yourself to wants,
But in an evil and unnatural stock.

sp.speaker: WALKADINE HOARD
sp.p: [To Gentlemen] Follow hard, gentlemen, follow hard!

lg.l: Is my love so deceiv’d? Before you all
I do renounce him; on my knees I vow
He ne’er shall marry me.

p.seg: Heaven knows he never meant it!

sp.speaker: WALKADINE HOARD
sp.p: [To Gentlemen] There, take her at the bound.

lg.l: Then, with a new and pure affection,
Behold yon gentleman, grave, kind, and rich,
A match worthy yourself. Esteeming him,
You do regard your state.
[To 1 Gentleman] I’ll make her a jointure, say.
He can join land to land and will possess you
Of what you can desire.
Come, widow, come.
The world is so deceitful.
There, ‘tis deceitful,
Where flattery, want, and imperfection lies.
But none of these in him. Push!
Pray, sir,—

sp.speaker: 1 GENTLEMAN
sp.p: Come, you widows are ever most backward when you should do yourselves most good; but were it to marry a chin not worth a hair now, then you would be forward enough. Come, clap hands, a match.

lg.l: With all my heart, widow. Thanks, gentlemen;
I will deserve your labour, and thy love.
Alas, you love not widows but for wealth.
I promise you I ha’ nothing, sir.
Well said, widow,
Well said! Thy love is all I seek, before
These gentlemen.
Now I must hope the best.

sp.speaker: WALKADINE HOARD
sp.p: My joys are such they want to be express’d.

sp.speaker: COURTESAN
sp.p: But, Master Hoard, one thing I must remember you of before these gentlemen, your friends: How shall I suddenly avoid the loathed soliciting of that perjur’d Witgood and his tedious, dissembling uncle, who this very, very day hath appointed a meeting for the same purpose too, where, had not truth come forth, I had been undone, utterly undone?

sp.speaker: WALKADINE HOARD
sp.p: What think you of that, gentlemen?

sp.speaker: 1 GENTLEMAN
sp.p: ‘Twas well devis’d.

sp.speaker: WALKADINE HOARD
sp.p: Hark thee, widow, train out young Witgood single; hasten him thither with thee, somewhat before the hour, where, at the place appointed, these gentlemen and myself will wait the opportunity, where by some sleight, removing him from thee, we’ll suddenly enter and surprise thee, carry thee away by boat to Cole Harbour, have a priest ready, and there clap it up instantly. How lik’st it, widow?

sp.speaker: COURTESAN
sp.p: In that it pleaseth you, it likes me well.

lg.l: I’ll kiss thee for those words. Come, gentlemen;
Still must I live a suitor to your favours,
Still to your aid beholding.
We’re engag’d, sir;
‘Tis for our credits now to see’t well ended.
‘Tis for your honours, gentlemen. Nay, look to’t.
Not only in joy, but I in wealth excel.
No more sweet widow, but sweet wife, farewell.

sp.speaker: COURTESAN
sp.p: Farewell, sir.

sp.speaker: WITGOOD
sp.p: Oh for more scope! I could laugh eternally. Give you joy, Mistress Hoard! I promis[‘d] your fortune was good, forsooth; y’ave fell upon wealth enough, and there’s young gentlemen enow can help you to the rest. Now it requires our wits. Carry thyself but heedfully now, and we are both—

sp.speaker: HOST
sp.p: Master Witgood, your uncle—

sp.speaker: WITGOOD
sp.p: Cuds me! Remove thyself a while; I’ll serve for him.

sp.speaker: LUCRE
sp.p: Nephew, good morrow, nephew.

sp.speaker: WITGOOD
sp.p: The same to you, kind uncle.

sp.speaker: LUCRE
sp.p: How fares the widow? Does the meeting hold?

sp.speaker: WITGOOD
sp.p: Oh, no question of that, sir.

sp.speaker: LUCRE
sp.p: I’ll strike the stroke then for thee; no more days.

sp.speaker: WITGOOD
sp.p: The sooner the better, uncle. Oh, she’s mightily followed.

sp.speaker: LUCRE
sp.p: And yet so little rumour’d.

sp.speaker: WITGOOD
sp.p: Mightily! Here comes one old gentleman, and he’ll make her a jointure of three hundred a year, forsooth; another wealthy suitor will estate his son in his lifetime, and make him weigh down the widow; here’s a merchant’s son will possess her with no less than three goodly lordships at once, which were all pawns to his father.

sp.speaker: LUCRE
sp.p: Peace, nephew, let me hear no more of ‘em; it mads me. Thou shalt prevent ‘em all. No words to the widow of my coming hither. Let me see, ‘tis now upon nine; before twelve, nephew, we will have the bargain struck. We will, faith, boy.

sp.speaker: WITGOOD
sp.p: Oh, my precious uncle!

sp.speaker: WALKADINE HOARD
sp.p: Niece, sweet niece, prithee have a care to my house. I leave all to thy discretion. Be content to dream awhile; I’ll have a husband for thee shortly. Put that care upon me, wench, for in choosing wives and husbands I am only fortunate; I have that gift given me.

lg.l: But ‘tis not likely you should choose for me,
Since nephew to your chiefest enemy
Is he whom I affect. But, O forgetful,
Why dost thou flatter thy affections so,
With name of him that for a widow’s bed
Neglects thy purer love? Can it be so,
Or does report dissemble?
How now, sir?
A letter, with which came a private charge.

sp.speaker: NIECE

lg.l: Therein I thank your care.
I know this hand.

sp.p: ‘Dearer than sight, what the world reports of me yet believe not. Rumour will alter shortly. Be thou constant. I am still the same that I was in love, and I hope to be the same in fortunes. Theodorus Witgood.’

lg.l: I am resolv’d. No more shall fear or doubt
Raise their pale powers to keep affection out.

div2.head: [ACT III SCENE 4]
div2.stage: Enter, with a Drawer, [Walkadine] Hoard and two Gentlemen Gentlemen Lawrence annotates “Perhaps Lamprey and Spitchcock” (p. 39).

sp.speaker: DRAWER
sp.p: You’re very welcome, gentlemen. Dick, show these gentlemen the Pom’granate there.

sp.speaker: WALKADINE HOARD
sp.p: Hist!

sp.speaker: DRAWER
sp.p: Up those stairs, gentlemen.

sp.speaker: WALKADINE HOARD
sp.p: Pist, drawer!

sp.speaker: DRAWER
sp.p: Anon, sir.

sp.speaker: WALKADINE HOARD
sp.p: Prithee, ask at the bar if a gentlewoman came not in lately.

sp.speaker: DRAWER
sp.p: William, at the bar! Did you see any gentlewoman come in lately? Speak you ay, speak you no?

sp.speaker: WITHIN
sp.p: No, none came in yet but Mistress Florence.

sp.speaker: DRAWER
sp.p: He says none came in yet, sir, but one Mistress Florence.

sp.speaker: WALKADINE HOARD
sp.p: What is that Florence? A widow?

sp.speaker: DRAWER
sp.p: Yes, a Dutch widow.

sp.speaker: WALKADINE HOARD
sp.p: How!

sp.speaker: DRAWER
sp.p: That’s an English drab, sir. Give your worship good morrow.

sp.speaker: WALKADINE HOARD
sp.p: A merry knave, i’ faith! I shall remember ‘a Dutch widow’ the longest day of my life.

sp.speaker: 1 GENTLEMAN
sp.p: Did not I use most art to win the widow?

sp.speaker: 2 GENTLEMAN
sp.p: You shall pardon me for that, sir; Master Hoard knows I took her at best ‘vantage.

sp.speaker: WALKADINE HOARD
sp.p: What’s that, sweet gentlemen, what’s that?

sp.speaker: 2 GENTLEMAN
sp.p: He will needs bear me down that his art only wrought with the widow most.

sp.speaker: WALKADINE HOARD
sp.p: Oh, you did both well, gentlemen, you did both well, I thank you.

lg.l: I was the first that mov’d her.
You were, i’ faith.

sp.speaker: 2 GENTLEMAN
sp.p: But it was I that took her at the bound.

sp.speaker: WALKADINE HOARD
sp.p: Ay, that was you; faith, gentlemen, ‘tis right.

sp.speaker: 1 GENTLEMAN
sp.p: I boasted least, but ‘twas I join’d their hands.

sp.speaker: WALKADINE HOARD
sp.p: By th’ mass, I think he did. You did all well, Gentlemen, you did all well. Contend no more.

lg.l: Come, yon room’s fittest.
True, ‘tis next the door.

sp.speaker: DRAWER
sp.p: You’re very welcome. Please you to walk upstairs; cloth’s laid, sir.

sp.speaker: COURTESAN
sp.p: Upstairs? Troth, I am weary, Master Witgood.

sp.speaker: WITGOOD
sp.p: Rest yourself here awhile, widow. We’ll have a cup of muscadine in this little room.

sp.speaker: DRAWER
sp.p: A cup of muscadine? You shall have the best, sir.

sp.speaker: WITGOOD
sp.p: But, do you hear, sirrah?

sp.speaker: DRAWER
sp.p: Do you call? Anon, sir.

sp.speaker: WITGOOD
sp.p: What is there provided for dinner?

sp.speaker: DRAWER
sp.p: I cannot readily tell you, sir. If you please, you may go into the kitchen and see yourself, sir. Many gentlemen of worship do use to do it, I assure you, sir.

sp.speaker: HOST
sp.p: A pretty familiar, priggin’ rascal! He has his part without book.

sp.speaker: WITGOOD
sp.p: Against you are ready to drink to me, widow, I’ll be present to pledge you.

sp.speaker: COURTESAN
sp.p: Nay, I commend your care; ‘tis done well of you. [Exit Witgood] Alas, what have I forgot?

sp.speaker: HOST
sp.p: What, mistress?

sp.speaker: COURTESAN
sp.p: I slipp’d my wedding ring off when I wash’d, and left it at my lodging. Prithee, run. I shall be sad without it. [Exit Host] So, he’s gone. Boy!

sp.speaker: BOY
sp.p: Anon, forsooth.

sp.speaker: COURTESAN
sp.p: Come hither, sirrah. Learn secretly if one Master Hoard, an ancient gentleman, be about house.

sp.speaker: BOY
sp.p: I heard such a one nam’d.

sp.speaker: COURTESAN
sp.p: Commend me to him.

sp.speaker: WALKADINE HOARD
sp.p: I’ll do thy commendations.

sp.speaker: COURTESAN
sp.p: Oh, you come well. Away! To boat! Begone!

sp.speaker: WALKADINE HOARD
sp.p: Thus wise men are reveng’d, give two for one.

lg.l: I must request
You, sir, to show extraordinary care.
My uncle comes with gentlemen, his friends,
And ‘tis upon a making.
Is it so?
I’ll give a special charge, good Master Witgood.
May I be bold to see her?
Who, the widow?
With all my heart, i’ faith. I’ll bring you to her.

sp.speaker: VINTNER
sp.p: If she be a Staffordshire gentlewoman, ‘tis much if I know her not.

sp.speaker: WITGOOD
sp.p: How now? Boy! Drawer!

sp.speaker: VINTNER
sp.p: Hie!

sp.speaker: BOY
sp.p: Do you call, sir?

sp.speaker: WITGOOD
sp.p: Went the gentlewoman up that was here?

sp.speaker: BOY
sp.p: Up, sir? She went out, sir.

sp.speaker: WITGOOD
sp.p: Out, sir?

sp.speaker: BOY
sp.p: Out, sir. One Master Hoard, with a guard of gentlemen, carried her out at back door a pretty while since, sir.

sp.speaker: WITGOOD
sp.p: Hoard? Death and darkness! Hoard?

sp.speaker: HOST
sp.p: The devil of ring I can find!

sp.speaker: WITGOOD
sp.p: How now? What news? Where’s the widow?

sp.speaker: HOST
sp.p: My mistress? Is she not here, sir?

lg.l: More madness yet!
She sent me for a ring.

sp.speaker: WITGOOD
sp.p: A plot, a plot! To boat! She’s stole away.

sp.speaker: HOST
sp.p: What?

div2.stage: Enter Lucre with Gentlemen Gentlemen Lawrence annotates “Friends to Lucre” (p. 42).

sp.speaker: WITGOOD
sp.p: Follow! Inquire! Old Hoard, my uncle’s adversary,—

lg.l: Nephew, what’s that?
Thrice-miserable wretch!
Why, what’s the matter?
The widow’s borne away, sir.

sp.speaker: LUCRE
sp.p: Ha! Passion of me! A heavy welcome, gentlemen.

sp.speaker: 1 GENTLEMAN
sp.p: The widow gone?

sp.speaker: LUCRE
sp.p: Who durst attempt it?

sp.speaker: WITGOOD
sp.p: Who but old Hoard, my uncle’s adversary?

sp.speaker: LUCRE
sp.p: How!

sp.speaker: WITGOOD
sp.p: With his confederates.

lg.l: Hoard, my deadly enemy! Gentlemen, stand to me.
I will not bear it. ‘Tis in hate of me
That villain seeks my shame, nay, thirsts my blood.
He owes me mortal malice.
I’ll spend my wealth on this despiteful plot,
Ere he shall cross me and my nephew thus.

sp.speaker: WITGOOD
sp.p: So maliciously!

sp.speaker: LUCRE
sp.p: How now, you treacherous rascal?

sp.speaker: HOST
sp.p: That’s none of my name, sir.

sp.speaker: WITGOOD
sp.p: Poor soul, he knew not on’t.

lg.l: I’m sorry. I see then ‘twas a mere plot.
I trac’d ‘em nearly,—
Well?
And hear for certain
They have took Cole Harbour.
The devil’s sanctuary!
They shall not rest. I’ll pluck her from his arms.
Kind and dear gentlemen,
If ever I had seat within your breasts,—
No more, good sir. It is a wrong to us
To see you injur’d. In a cause so just
We’ll spend our lives, but we will right our friends.
Honest and kind! Come, we have delay’d too long.
Nephew, take comfort; a just cause is strong.
That’s all my comfort, uncle.
Ha, ha, ha!
Now may events fall luckily and well;
He that ne’er strives, says wit, shall ne’er excel.

sp.speaker: DAMPIT
sp.p: When did I say my prayers? In anno ‘88, when the great armada was coming, and in anno ‘99, when the great thund’ring and lightning was. I pray’d heartily then, i’ faith, to overthrow Povey’s new buildings. I kneel’d by my great iron chest, I remember.

sp.speaker: AUDREY
sp.p: Master Dampit, one may hear you before they see you. You keep sweet hours, Master Dampit. We were all abed three hours ago.

sp.speaker: DAMPIT
sp.p: Audrey?

sp.speaker: AUDREY
sp.p: Oh, y’are a fine gentleman!

sp.speaker: DAMPIT
sp.p: So I am, i’ faith, and a fine scholar. Do you use to go to bed so early, Audrey?

sp.speaker: AUDREY
sp.p: Call you this early, Master Dampit?

sp.speaker: DAMPIT
sp.p: Why, is’t not one of clock i’ th’ morning? Is not that early enough? Fetch me a glass of fresh beer.

sp.speaker: AUDREY
sp.p: Here, I have warm’d your nightcap for you, Master Dampit.

sp.speaker: DAMPIT
sp.p: Draw it on then, I am very weak truly. I have not eaten so much as the bulk of an egg these three days.

sp.speaker: AUDREY
sp.p: You have drunk the more, Master Dampit.

sp.speaker: DAMPIT
sp.p: What’s that?

sp.speaker: AUDREY
sp.p: You mought and you would, Master Dampit.

sp.speaker: DAMPIT
sp.p: I answer you, I cannot. Hold your prating. You prate too much and understand too little. Are you answered? Give me a glass of beer.

sp.speaker: AUDREY
sp.p: May I ask you how you do, Master Dampit?

sp.speaker: DAMPIT
sp.p: How do I? I’ faith, naught.

sp.speaker: AUDREY
sp.p: I ne’er knew you do otherwise.

sp.speaker: DAMPIT
sp.p: I eat not one penn’ort’ of bread these two years. Give me a glass of fresh beer, I am not sick, nor I am not well.

sp.speaker: AUDREY
sp.p: Take this warm napkin about your neck, sir, whilst I help you make you unready.

sp.speaker: DAMPIT
sp.p: How now, Audrey-prater, with your scurvy devices, what say you now?

sp.speaker: AUDREY
sp.p: What say I, Master Dampit? I say nothing but that you are very weak.

sp.speaker: DAMPIT
sp.p: Faith, thou hast more cony-catching devices than all London.

sp.speaker: AUDREY
sp.p: Why, Master Dampit, I never deceiv’d you in all my life.

sp.speaker: DAMPIT
sp.p: Why was that? Because I never did trust thee.

sp.speaker: AUDREY
sp.p: I care not what you say, Master Dampit.

sp.speaker: DAMPIT
sp.p: Hold thy prating. I answer thee, thou art a beggar, a quean, and a bawd. Are you answer’d?

sp.speaker: AUDREY
sp.p: Fie, Master Dampit! A gentleman, and have such words!

sp.speaker: DAMPIT
sp.p: Why, thou base drudge of infortunity, thou kitchen-stuff drab of beggary, roguery, and coxcombry, thou cavernesed quean of foolery, knavery, and bawdreaminy, I’ll tell thee what, I will not give a louse for thy fortunes.

sp.speaker: AUDREY
sp.p: No, Master Dampit, and there’s a gentleman comes a-wooing to me, and he doubts nothing but that you will get me from him.

sp.speaker: DAMPIT
sp.p: I? If I would either have thee or lie with thee for two thousand pound, would I might be damn’d! Why, thou base, impudent quean of foolery, flattery, and coxcombry, are you answer’d?

sp.speaker: AUDREY
sp.p: Come, will you rise and go to bed, sir?

sp.speaker: DAMPIT
sp.p: Rise and go to bed too, Audrey. How does Mistress Proserpine?

sp.speaker: AUDREY
sp.p: Fooh!

sp.speaker: DAMPIT
sp.p: She’s as fine a philosopher of a stinkard’s wife as any within the liberties. Faugh, faugh, Audrey!

sp.speaker: AUDREY
sp.p: How now, Master Dampit?

sp.speaker: DAMPIT
sp.p: Fie upon’t, what a choice of stinks here is! What hast thou done, Audrey? Fie upon’t, here’s a choice of stinks indeed! Give me a glass of fresh beer, and then I will to bed.

sp.speaker: AUDREY
sp.p: It waits for you above, sir.

sp.speaker: DAMPIT
sp.p: Fooh, I think they burn horns in Barnard’s Inn. If ever I smell’d such an abominable stink, usury forsake me.

sp.speaker: AUDREY
sp.p: They be the stinking nails of his trampling feet, and he talks of burning of horns.

div2.head: <<Incipit>> ACT IV [SCENE 1]
div2.stage: Enter, at Cole Harbour, [Walkadine] Hoard, the Widow, and Gentlemen, Gentlemen, Lawrence annotates “Spitchcock and Lamprey” (p. 45), but editors since Michael Taylor (1995) assign the first speech to Lamprey. he married now

lg.l: Join hearts, join hands,
In wedlock’s bands;
Never to part,
Till death cleave your heart.
You shall forsake all other women;
You, lords, knights, gentlemen, and yeomen.
What my tongue slips
Make up with your lips.
Give you joy, Mistress Hoard; let the kiss come about.
Who knocks? Convey my little pig-eater out.
[Within] Hoard!
Upon my life, my adversary, gentlemen!
[Within] Hoard, open the door or we will force it ope.
Give us the widow.
Gentlemen, keep ‘em out.
He comes upon his death that enters here.
[Within] My friends, assist me.
He has assistants, gentlemen.
Tut! Nor him nor them, we in this action fear.
[Within] Shall I in peace speak one word with the widow?
Husband and gentlemen, hear me but a word.
Freely, sweet wife.
Let him in peaceably;
You know we’re sure from any act of his.
Most true.
You may stand by and smile at his old weakness.
Let me alone to answer him.
Content.
‘Twill be good mirth, i’ faith. How think you, gentlemen?
Good gullery!
Upon calm conditions, let him in.
[Within] All spite and malice—
Hear me, Master Lucre.
So you will vow a peaceful entrance
With those your friends, and only exercise
Calm conference with the widow, without fury,
The passage shall receive you.
[Within] I do vow it.
Then enter and talk freely. Here she stands.

div2.stage: Enter Lucre [, his friends, and Host]

lg.l: Oh, Master Hoard, your spite has watch’d the hour.
You’re excellent at vengeance, Master Hoard.

sp.speaker: WALKADINE HOARD
sp.p: Ha, ha, ha!

lg.l: I am the fool you laugh at.
You are wise, sir, and know the seasons. Well,
Come hither, widow.
Why, is it thus?
Oh, you have done me infinite disgrace
And your own credit no small injury.
Suffer mine enemy so despitefully
To bear you from my nephew? Oh, I had
Rather half my substance had been forfeit
And begg’d by some starv’d rascal.
Why, what would you wish me do, sir?
I must not overthrow my state for love;
We have too many precedents for that.
From thousands of our wealthy undone widows
One may derive some wit. I do confess
I lov’d your nephew; nay, I did affect him
Against the mind and liking of my friends,
Believ’d his promises, lay here in hope
Of flatter’d living and the boast of lands.
Coming to touch his wealth and state indeed,
It appears dross. I find him not the man;
Imperfect, mean, scarce furnish’d of his needs.
In words, fair lordships; in performance, hovels.
Can any woman love the thing that is not?
Broke you for this?
Was it not cause too much?
Send to inquire his state. Most part of it
Lay two years mortgag’d in his uncle’s hands.
Why, say it did. You might have known my mind;
I could have soon restor’d it.
Ay. Had I but seen any such thing perform’d,
Why, ‘twould have tied my affection and contain’d
Me in my first desires. Do you think, i’ faith,
That I could twine such a dry oak as this,
Had promise in your nephew took effect?
Why, and there’s no time pass’d, and rather than
My adversary should thus thwart my hopes,
I would—
Tut! Y’ave been ever full of golden speech.
If words were lands, your nephew would be rich.
Widow, believe it, I vow by my best bliss,
Before these gentlemen, I will give in
The mortgage to my nephew instantly,
Before I sleep or eat.

sp.speaker: 1 GENTLEMAN GENTLEMAN Lawrence annotates “A friend to Lucre” (p. 47).

lg.l: We’ll pawn our credits,
Widow, what he speaks shall be perform’d
In fullness.
Nay, more. I will estate him
In farther blessings: He shall be my heir.
I have no son.
I’ll bind myself to that condition.
When I shall hear this done I shall soon yield
To reasonable terms.
In the mean season,
Will you protest, before these gentlemen,
To keep yourself as you are now at this present?
I do protest, before these gentlemen,
I will be as clear then as I am now.
I do believe you. Here’s your own honest servant;
I’ll take him along with me.
Ay, with all my heart.
He shall see all perform’d, and bring you word.
That’s all I wait for.

sp.speaker: WALKADINE HOARD
sp.p: What, have you finish’d, Master Lucre? Ha, ha, ha, ha!

lg.l: So, laugh, Hoard, laugh at your poor enemy, do.
The wind may turn; you may be laugh’d at too!
Yes, marry, may you, sir. Ha, ha, ha!
Ha, ha, ha! If every man that swells in malice
Could be reveng’d as happily as I,
He would choose hate and forswear amity.
What did he say, wife, prithee?
Faith, spoke to ease his mind.
Oh, oh, oh!
You know now, little to any purpose.
True, true, true.
He would do mountains now.
Ay, ay, ay, ay.
Y’ave struck him dead, Master Hoard.
Ay, and his nephew desperate.
I know’t, sirs, ay.
Never did man so crush his enemy.

div2.head: [ACT IV SCENE 2]
div2.stage: Enter Lucre with Gentlemen Gentlemen Lawrence annotates “Friends to Lucre” (p. 49). [and Host], meeting Sam Freedom

sp.speaker: LUCRE
sp.p: My son-in-law, Sam Freedom, where’s my nephew?

sp.speaker: SAM
sp.p: O man in lamentation, father!

sp.speaker: LUCRE
sp.p: How!

sp.speaker: SAM
sp.p: He thumps his breast like a gallant dicer that has lost his doublet, and stands in’s shirt to do penance.

sp.speaker: LUCRE
sp.p: Alas, poor gentleman!

sp.speaker: SAM
sp.p: I warrant you may hear him sigh in a still evening to your house at Highgate.

sp.speaker: LUCRE
sp.p: I prithee, send him in.

sp.speaker: SAM
sp.p: Were it to do a greater matter, I will not stick with you, sir, in regard you married my mother.

sp.speaker: LUCRE
sp.p: Sweet gentlemen, cheer him up. I will but fetch the mortgage and return to you instantly.

lg.l: We’ll do our best, sir. See where he comes,
E’en joyless and regardless of all form.

sp.speaker: 2 GENTLEMAN
sp.p: Why, how, Master Witgood! Fie! You a firm scholar and an understanding gentleman, and give your best parts to passion?

sp.speaker: 1 GENTLEMAN
sp.p: Come, fie!

sp.speaker: WITGOOD
sp.p: Oh, gentlemen,—

lg.l: Sorrow of me, what a sigh was there, sir!
Nine such widows are not worth it.
To be borne from me by that lecher, Hoard!
That vengeance is your uncle’s, being done
More in despite to him than wrong to you,
But we bring comfort now.
I beseech you, gentlemen,—
Cheer thyself, man; there’s hope of her, i’ faith.
Too gladsome to be true.
Nephew, what cheer?
Alas, poor gentleman, how art thou chang’d!
Call thy fresh blood into thy cheeks again.
She comes—
Nothing afflicts me so much
But that it is your adversary, uncle,
And merely plotted in despite of you.

sp.speaker: LUCRE
sp.p: Ay, that’s it mads me, spites me. I’ll spend my wealth ere he shall carry her so, because I know ‘tis only to spite me. Ay, this is it. Here, nephew, before these kind gentlemen, I deliver in your mortgage, my promise to the widow. See, ‘tis done. Be wise. You’re once more master of your own; the widow shall perceive now you are not altogether such a beggar as the world reputes you. You can make shift to bring her to three hundred a year, sir.

lg.l: By’r lady, and that’s no toy, sir.
A word, nephew.

sp.speaker: 1 GENTLEMAN
sp.p: Now you may certify the widow.

lg.l: You must conceive it aright, nephew, now.
To do you good, I am content to do this.
I know it, sir.
But your own conscience can tell I had it
Dearly enough of you.
Ay, that’s most certain.
Much money laid out, beside many a journey
To fetch the rent. I hope you’ll think on’t, nephew.
I were worse than a beast else, i’ faith.
Although to blind the widow and the world,
I out of policy do’t, yet there’s a conscience, nephew.
Heaven forbid else!
When you are full possess’d,
‘Tis nothing to return it.
Alas, a thing quickly done, uncle.
Well said. You know I give it you but in trust.
Pray let me understand you rightly, uncle:
You give it me but in trust?
No.
That is, you trust me with it.
True, true.

l.seg: But if ever I trust you with it again,
Would I might be truss’d up for my labour.

sp.speaker: LUCRE
sp.p: You can all witness, gentlemen, and you, sir yeoman.

sp.speaker: HOST
sp.p: My life for yours, sir, now. I know my mistress’ mind too well toward your nephew. Let things be in preparation, and I’ll train her hither in most excellent fashion.

sp.speaker: LUCRE
sp.p: A good old boy.—Wife! Jenny!

sp.speaker: WIFE
sp.p: What’s the news, sir?

sp.speaker: LUCRE
sp.p: The wedding day’s at hand! Prithee, sweet wife, express thy housewifery. Thou’rt a fine cook, I know’t; thy first husband married thee out of an alderman’s kitchen. Go to! He rais’d thee for raising of paste. What! Here’s none but friends. Most of our beginnings must be wink’d at. Gentlemen, I invite you all to my nephew’s wedding against Thursday morning.

lg.l: With all our hearts, and we shall joy to see
Your enemy so mock’d.
He laugh’d at me, gentlemen; ha, ha, ha.
He has no conscience, faith, would laugh at them.
They laugh at one another.
Who then can be so cruel? Troth, not I;
I rather pity now than aught envy.
I do conceive such joy in mine own happiness,
I have no leisure yet to laugh at their follies.
Thou soul of my estate, I kiss thee,
I miss life’s comfort when I miss thee.
Oh, never will we part again,
Until I leave the sight of men.
We’ll ne’er trust conscience of own kin,
Since cozenage brings that title in.

sp.speaker: 1 CREDITOR
sp.p: I’ll wait these seven hours, but I’ll see him caught.

sp.speaker: 2 CREDITOR
sp.p: Faith, so will I.

sp.speaker: 3 CREDITOR
sp.p: Hang him, prodigal! He’s stripp’d of the widow.

sp.speaker: 1 CREDITOR
sp.p: A’ my troth, she’s the wiser; she has made the happier choice, and I wonder of what stuff those widows’ hearts are made of, that will marry unfledg’d boys, before comely thrum-chinn’d gentlemen.

sp.speaker: BOY
sp.p: News, news, news!

sp.speaker: 1 CREDITOR
sp.p: What, boy?

sp.speaker: BOY
sp.p: The rioter is caught!

lg.l: So, so, so, so. It warms me at the heart.
I love a’ life to see dogs upon men.
Oh, here he comes.

sp.speaker: WITGOOD
sp.p: My last joy was so great it took away the sense of all future afflictions. What a day is here o’ercast! How soon a black tempest rises!

sp.speaker: 1 CREDITOR
sp.p: Oh, we may speak with you now, sir. What’s become of your rich widow? I think you may cast your cap at the widow, may you not, sir?

sp.speaker: 2 CREDITOR
sp.p: He, a rich widow? Who, a prodigal, a daily rioter, and a nightly vomiter? He, a widow of account? He, a hole i’ th’ Counter!

sp.speaker: WITGOOD
sp.p: You do well, my masters, to tyrannize over misery, to afflict the afflicted. ‘Tis a custom you have here amongst you. I would wish you never leave it, and I hope you’ll do as I bid you.

sp.speaker: 1 CREDITOR
sp.p: Come, come, sir; what say you extempore now to your bill of a hundred pound? A sweet debt for frotting your doublets.

sp.speaker: 2 CREDITOR
sp.p: Here’s mine of forty.

sp.speaker: 3 CREDITOR
sp.p: Here’s mine of fifty.

sp.speaker: WITGOOD
