sp.p: Pray, sirs, you’ll give me breath?

sp.speaker: 1 CREDITOR
sp.p: No, sir, we’ll keep you out of breath still. Then we shall be sure you will not run away from us.

sp.speaker: WITGOOD
sp.p: Will you but hear me speak?

sp.speaker: 2 CREDITOR
sp.p: You shall pardon us for that, sir. We know you have too fair a tongue of your own; you overcame us too lately, a shame take you. We are like to lose all that for want of witnesses. We dealt in policy then. Always when we strive to be most politic we prove most coxcombs, non plus ultra . I perceive by us, we’re not ordain’d to thrive by wisdom, and therefore we must be content to be tradesmen.

sp.speaker: WITGOOD
sp.p: Give me but reasonable time, and I protest I’ll make you ample satisfaction.

sp.speaker: 1 CREDITOR
sp.p: Do you talk of reasonable time to us?

sp.speaker: WITGOOD
sp.p: ‘Tis true, beasts know no reasonable time.

sp.speaker: 2 CREDITOR
sp.p: We must have either money or carcass.

sp.speaker: WITGOOD
sp.p: Alas, what good will my carcass do you?

sp.speaker: 3 CREDITOR
sp.p: Oh, ‘tis a secret delight we have amongst us. We that are used to keep birds in cages have the heart to keep men in prison, I warrant you.

p.seg: I perceive I must crave a little more aid from my wits: Do but make shift for me this once, and I’ll forswear ever to trouble you in the like fashion hereafter. I’ll have better employment for you and I live.

sp.speaker: 1 CREDITOR
sp.p: That’s our desires, sir.

sp.speaker: HOST
sp.p: Master Witgood?

sp.speaker: WITGOOD
sp.p: Oh, art thou come?

sp.speaker: HOST
sp.p: May I speak one word with you in private, sir?

sp.speaker: WITGOOD
sp.p: No, by my faith, canst thou. I am in Hell here, and the devils will not let me come to thee.

sp.speaker: CITIZENS
sp.p: Do you call us devils? You shall find us puritans! Bear him away. Let ‘em talk as they go. We’ll not stand to hear ‘em. Ah, sir, am I a devil? I shall think the better of myself as long as I live. A devil, i’ faith!

sp.speaker: WALKADINE HOARD
sp.p: What a sweet blessing hast thou, Master Hoard, above a multitude! Wilt thou never be thankful? How dost thou think to be bless’d another time? Or dost thou count this the full measure of thy happiness? By my troth, I think thou dost. Not only a wife large in possessions, but spacious in content. She’s rich, she’s young, she’s fair, she’s wise. When I wake, I think of her lands; that revives me. When I go to bed, I dream of her beauty, and that’s enough for me. She’s worth four hundred a year in her very smock, if a man knew how to use it. But the journey will be all, in troth, into the country; to ride to her lands in state and order, following my brother and other worshipful gentlemen, whose companies I ha’ sent down for already, to ride along with us in their goodly decorum beards, their broad velvet cassocks, and chains of gold twice or thrice double. Against which time I’ll entertain some ten men of mine own into liveries, all of occupations or qualities. I will not keep an idle man about me. The sight of which will so vex my adversary Lucre, for we’ll pass by his door of purpose, make a little stand for [the] nonce, and have our horses curvet before the window. Certainly he will never endure it, but run up and hang himself presently. [Enter Servant] How now, sirrah? What news? Any that offer their service to me yet?

sp.speaker: SERVANT
sp.p: Yes, sir, there are some i’ th’ hall that wait for your worship’s liking, and desire to be entertain’d.

sp.speaker: WALKADINE HOARD
sp.p: Are they of occupation?

sp.speaker: SERVANT
sp.p: They are men fit for your worship, sir.

sp.speaker: WALKADINE HOARD
sp.p: Say’st so? Send ‘em all in. [Exit Servant] To see ten men ride after me in watchet liveries with orange-tawny capes, ‘twill cut his comb, i’ faith. Enter all [, Tailor, Barber, Perfumer, Falconer, and Huntsman] How now? Of what occupation are you, sir?

sp.speaker: TAILOR
sp.p: A tailor, an’t please your worship.

sp.speaker: WALKADINE HOARD
sp.p: A tailor? Oh, very good. You shall serve to make all the liveries.—What are you, sir?

sp.speaker: BARBER
sp.p: A barber, sir.

sp.speaker: WALKADINE HOARD
sp.p: A barber? Very needful. You shall shave all the house, and if need require, stand for a reaper i’ th’ summer time.—You, sir?

sp.speaker: PERFUMER
sp.p: A perfumer.

sp.speaker: WALKADINE HOARD
sp.p: I smell’d you before. Perfumers, of all men, had need carry themselves uprightly, for if they were once knaves they would be smell’d out quickly.—To you, sir?

sp.speaker: FALCONER
sp.p: A falc’ner, an’t please your worship.

sp.speaker: WALKADINE HOARD
sp.p: Sa ho, sa ho, sa ho!—and you, sir?

sp.speaker: HUNTSMAN
sp.p: A huntsman, sir.

sp.speaker: WALKADINE HOARD
sp.p: There, boy, there, boy, there, boy. I am not so old but I have pleasant days to come. I promise you, my masters, I take such a good liking to you that I entertain you all. I put you already into my countenance, and you shall be shortly in my livery. But especially you two, my jolly falc’ner and my bonny huntsman, we shall have most need of you at my wife’s manor houses i’ th’ country. There’s goodly parks and champion grounds for you. We shall have all our sports within ourselves. All the gentlemen a’ th’ country shall be beholding to us and our pastimes.

sp.speaker: FALCONER
sp.p: And we’ll make your worship admire, sir.

sp.speaker: WALKADINE HOARD
sp.p: Say’st thou so? Do but make me admire, and thou shalt want for nothing.—My tailor?

sp.speaker: TAILOR
sp.p: Anon, sir.

sp.speaker: WALKADINE HOARD
sp.p: Go presently in hand with the liveries.

sp.speaker: TAILOR
sp.p: I will, sir.

sp.speaker: WALKADINE HOARD
sp.p: My barber.

sp.speaker: BARBER
sp.p: Here, sir.

sp.speaker: WALKADINE HOARD
sp.p: Make ‘em all trim fellows, louse ‘em well, especially my huntsman, and cut all their beards of the Polonian fashion. —My perfumer?

sp.speaker: PERFUMER
sp.p: Under your nose, sir.

sp.speaker: WALKADINE HOARD
sp.p: Cast a better savour upon the knaves, to take away the scent of my tailor’s feet and my barber’s lotium water.

sp.speaker: PERFUMER
sp.p: It shall be carefully perform’d, sir.

sp.speaker: WALKADINE HOARD
sp.p: But you, my falc’ner and huntsman, the welcom’st men alive, i’ faith!

sp.speaker: HUNTSMAN
sp.p: And we’ll show you that, sir, shall deserve your worship’s favour.

sp.speaker: WALKADINE HOARD
sp.p: I prithee, show me that. Go, you knaves all, and wash your lungs i’ th’ buttery, go. [Exeunt Tailor, Barber, Perfumer, Falconer, and Huntsman.] By th’ mass, and well rememb’red. I’ll ask my wife that question. Wife! Mistress Jane Hoard!

sp.speaker: COURTESAN
sp.p: Sir, would you with me?

sp.speaker: WALKADINE HOARD
sp.p: I would but know, sweet wife, which might stand best to thy liking, to have the wedding dinner kept here or i’ th’ country?

sp.speaker: COURTESAN
sp.p: Hum. Faith, sir, ‘twould like me better here. Here you were married, here let all rites be ended.

sp.speaker: WALKADINE HOARD
sp.p: Could a marquess give a better answer? Hoard, bear thy head aloft, thou’st a wife will advance it. [Enter Host with a letter] What haste comes here now? Yes, a letter, some dreg of my adversary’s malice. Come hither. What’s the news?

sp.speaker: HOST
sp.p: A thing that concerns my mistress, sir.

sp.speaker: WALKADINE HOARD
sp.p: Why, then it concerns me, knave.

sp.speaker: HOST
sp.p: Ay, and you, knave, too—cry your worship mercy. You are both like to come into trouble, I promise you, sir: a precontract.

sp.speaker: WALKADINE HOARD
sp.p: How! A precontract, say’st thou?

sp.speaker: HOST
sp.p: I fear they have too much proof on’t, sir. Old Lucre, he runs mad up and down, and will to law as fast as he can. Young Witgood, laid hold on by his creditors, he exclaims upon you a’ tother side, says you have wrought his undoing by the injurious detaining of his contract.

sp.speaker: WALKADINE HOARD
sp.p: Body a’ me!

lg.l: He will have utmost satisfaction.
The law shall give him recompense he says.

p.seg: Alas, his creditors so merciless! My state being yet uncertain, I deem it not unconscionable to further him.

sp.speaker: HOST
sp.p: True, sir,—

sp.speaker: WALKADINE HOARD
sp.p: Wife, what says that letter? Let me construe it.

lg.l: Curs’d be my rash and unadvised words!
I’ll set my foot upon my tongue
And tread my inconsiderate grant to dust.

sp.speaker: WALKADINE HOARD
sp.p: Wife,—

p.seg: A pretty shift, i’ faith. I commend a woman when she can make away a letter from her husband handsomely, and this was cleanly done, by my troth.

lg.l: I did, sir.
Some foolish words I must confess did pass,
Which now litigiously he fastens on me.

sp.speaker: WALKADINE HOARD
sp.p: Of what force? Let me examine ‘em.

sp.speaker: COURTESAN
sp.p: Too strong, I fear. Would I were well freed of him.

sp.speaker: WALKADINE HOARD
sp.p: Shall I compound?

lg.l: No, sir, I’d have it done some nobler way
Of your side. I’d have you come off with honour;
Let baseness keep with them. Why, have you not
The means, sir? The occasion’s offer’d you.

sp.speaker: WALKADINE HOARD
sp.p: Where? How, dear wife?

sp.speaker: COURTESAN
sp.p: He is now caught by his creditors. The slave’s needy, his debts petty. He’ll rather bind himself to all inconveniences than rot in prison. By this only means you may get a release from him. ‘Tis not yet come to his uncle’s hearing. Send speedily for the creditors. By this time he’s desperate; he’ll set his hand to anything. Take order for his debts or discharge ‘em quite. A pax on him! Let’s be rid of a rascal.

lg.l: Excellent!
Thou dost astonish me.—Go, run, make haste!
Bring both the creditors and Witgood hither.

l.seg: This will be some revenge yet.

lg.l: In the mean space I’ll have a release drawn.—
Within there!
Sir?
Sirrah, come take directions. Go to my scrivener.

l.seg: I’m yet like those whose riches lie in dreams;
If I be wak’d, they’re false. Such is my fate,
Who ventures deeper than the desperate state.
Though I have sinn’d, yet could I become new,
For where I once vow, I am ever true.

sp.speaker: WALKADINE HOARD
sp.p: Away! Dispatch! On my displeasure, quickly! [Exit Servant.] Happy occasion! Pray Heaven he be in the right vein now to set his hand to’t, that nothing alter him. Grant that all his follies may meet in him at once, to besot him enough. I pray for him, i’ faith, and here he comes.

sp.speaker: WITGOOD
sp.p: What would you with me now, my uncle’s spiteful adversary?

lg.l: Nay, I am friends.
Ay, when your mischief’s spent.
I heard you were arrested.
Well, what then?
You will pay none of my debts, I am sure.
A wise man cannot tell.
There may be those conditions ‘greed upon
May move me to do much.
Ay, when?
‘Tis thou, perjured woman! Oh, no name
Is vild enough to match thy treachery,
That art the cause of my confusion.
Out, you
Penurious slave!
Nay, wife, you are too forward.
Let him alone. Give losers leave to talk.
Shall I remember thee of another promise
Far stronger than the first?
I’d fain know that.
‘Twould call shame to thy cheeks.
Shame?

sp.speaker: WITGOOD

lg.l: Hark in your ear.

sp.p: [To Courtesan] Will he come off, think’st thou, and pay my debts roundly?

sp.speaker: COURTESAN
sp.p: [To Witgood] Doubt nothing. There’s a release a-drawing and all, to which you must set your hand.

sp.speaker: WITGOOD
sp.p: [To Courtesan] Excellent!

sp.speaker: COURTESAN
sp.p: [To Witgood] But methinks, i’ faith, you might have made some shift to discharge this yourself, having in the mortgage, and never have burden’d my conscience with it.

sp.speaker: WITGOOD
sp.p: [To Courtesan] A’ my troth, I could not, for my creditors’ cruelties extend to the present.

sp.speaker: COURTESAN
sp.p: [To Witgood] No more.—Why, do your worst for that, I defy you.

sp.speaker: WITGOOD
sp.p: Y’are impudent! I’ll call up witnesses.

lg.l: Call up thy wits, for thou hast been devoted
To follies a long time.

sp.speaker: WALKADINE HOARD

lg.l: Wife, y’are too bitter.

sp.p: Master Witgood, and you, my masters, you shall hear a mild speech come from me now, and this it is: ‘Thas been my fortune, gentlemen, to have an extraordinary blessing pour’d upon me a’ late, and here she stands. I have wedded her and bedded her, and yet she is little the worse. Some foolish words she hath pass’d to you in the country, and some peevish debts you owe here in the city. Set the hare’s head to the goose-giblet. Release you her of her words, and I’ll release you of your debts, sir.

sp.speaker: WITGOOD
sp.p: Would you so? I thank you for that, sir. I cannot blame you, i’ faith.

sp.speaker: WALKADINE HOARD
sp.p: Why, are not debts better than words, sir?

sp.speaker: WITGOOD
sp.p: Are not words promises, and are not promises debts, sir?

p.seg: He plays at back-racket with me.

sp.speaker: 1 CREDITOR
sp.p: Come hither, Master Witgood, come hither. Be rul’d by fools once.

sp.speaker: 2 CREDITOR
sp.p: We are citizens and know what belong[s] to’t.

sp.speaker: 1 CREDITOR
sp.p: Take hold of his offer. Pax on her! Let her go. If your debts were once discharg’d, I would help you to a widow myself worth ten of her.

sp.speaker: 3 CREDITOR
sp.p: Mass, partner, and now you remember me on’t, there’s Master Mulligrub’s sister newly fall’n a widow.

sp.speaker: 1 CREDITOR
sp.p: Cuds me, as pat as can be. There’s a widow left for you; ten thousand in money, beside plate, jewels, et cetera . I warrant it a match. We can do all in all with her. Prithee, dispatch. We’ll carry thee to her presently.

sp.speaker: WITGOOD
sp.p: My uncle will ne’er endure me when he shall hear I set my hand to a release.

sp.speaker: 2 CREDITOR
sp.p: Hark, I’ll tell thee a trick for that. I have spent five hundred pound in suits in my time, I should be wise. Thou’rt now a prisoner; make a release. Take’t of my word, whatsoever a man makes as long as he is in durance, ‘tis nothing in law, not thus much.

sp.speaker: WITGOOD
sp.p: Say you so, sir?

sp.speaker: 3 CREDITOR
sp.p: I have paid for’t, I know’t.

sp.speaker: WITGOOD
sp.p: Proceed then. I consent.

sp.speaker: 3 CREDITOR
sp.p: Why, well said.

sp.speaker: WALKADINE HOARD
sp.p: How now, my masters, what have you done with him?

sp.speaker: 1 CREDITOR
sp.p: With much ado, sir, we have got him to consent.

sp.speaker: WALKADINE HOARD
sp.p: Ah, ah, ah! And what came his debts to now?

sp.speaker: 1 CREDITOR
sp.p: Some eight score odd pounds, sir.

sp.speaker: WALKADINE HOARD
sp.p: Naw, naw, naw, naw, naw. Tell me the second time. Give me a lighter sum. They are but desperate debts, you know, ne’er call’d in but upon such an accident. A poor, needy knave, he would starve and rot in prison. Come, come, you shall have ten shillings in the pound, and the sum down roundly—

sp.speaker: 1 CREDITOR
sp.p: You must make it a mark, sir.

sp.speaker: WALKADINE HOARD
sp.p: Go to, then. Tell your money in the meantime; you shall find little less there. [Gives them money] —Come, Master Witgood, you are so unwilling to do yourself good now. [Enter Scrivener] Welcome, honest scrivener. Now you shall hear the release read.

sp.speaker: SCRIVENER
sp.p: ‘Be it known to all men by these presents that I, Theodorus Witgood, gentleman, sole nephew to Pecunius Lucre, having unjustly made title and claim to one Jane Medlar, late widow of Anthony Medlar, and now wife to Walkadine Hoard, in consideration of a competent sum of money to discharge my debts, do for ever hereafter disclaim any title, right, estate, or interest in or to the said widow, late in the occupation of the said Anthony Medlar and now in the occupation of Walkadine Hoard; as also neither to lay claim, by virtue of any former contract, grant, promise or demise, to any of her manor[s], manor houses, parks, groves, meadow grounds, arable lands, barns, stacks, stables, dove holes, and cony burrows, together with all her cattle, money, plate, jewels, borders, chains, bracelets, furnitures, hangings, movables, or immovables. In witness whereof, I, the said Theodorus Witgood, have interchangeably set to my hand and seal before these presents, the day and date above written.’

sp.speaker: WITGOOD
sp.p: What a precious fortune hast thou slipp’d here, like a beast as thou art!

sp.speaker: WALKADINE HOARD
sp.p: Come, unwilling heart, come.

lg.l: Well, Master Hoard, give me the pen; I see
‘Tis vain to quarrel with our destiny.

sp.speaker: WALKADINE HOARD
sp.p: Oh, as vain a thing as can be. You cannot commit a greater absurdity, sir. So, so, give me that hand now. Before all these presents, I am friends for ever with thee.

sp.speaker: WITGOOD
sp.p: Troth, and it were pity of my heart now if I should bear you any grudge, i’ faith.

sp.speaker: WALKADINE HOARD
sp.p: Content. I’ll send for thy uncle against the wedding dinner. We will be friends once again.

sp.speaker: WITGOOD
sp.p: I hope to bring it to pass myself, sir.

sp.speaker: WALKADINE HOARD
sp.p: How now? Is’t right, my masters?

sp.speaker: 1 CREDITOR
sp.p: ‘Tis something wanting, sir, yet it shall be sufficient.

sp.speaker: WALKADINE HOARD
sp.p: Why, well said. A good conscience makes a fine show nowadays. Come, my masters, you shall all taste of my wine ere you depart.

sp.speaker: ALL
sp.p: We follow you, sir.

p.seg: I’ll try these fellows now.

sp.speaker: 1 CREDITOR
sp.p: Why, do you think we were in earnest, i’ faith? Carry you to a rich widow? We should get much credit by that! A noted rioter, a contemptible prodigal! ‘Twas a trick we have amongst us to get in our money. Fare you well, sir.

sp.speaker: WITGOOD
sp.p: Farewell and be hang’d, you short pig-hair’d, ram-headed rascals! He that believes in you shall ne’er be sav’d, I warrant him. By this new league I shall have some access unto my love.

sp.speaker: NIECE
sp.p: Master Witgood!

sp.speaker: WITGOOD
sp.p: My life!

sp.speaker: NIECE
sp.p: Meet me presently. That note directs you. I would not be suspected. Our happiness attends us. Farewell.

sp.speaker: WITGOOD
sp.p: A word’s enough.

div2.head: [ACT IV SCENE 5]
div2.stage: Dampit the usurer in his bed, Audrey spinning by

lg.l: Song. Let the usurer cram him, in interest that excel,
There’s pits enow to damn him before he comes to Hell.
In Holborn some, in Fleet Street some,
Where’er he come, there’s some, there’s some.

sp.speaker: DAMPIT
sp.p: Trahe, trahito , draw the curtain. Give me a sip of sack more.

div2.stage: Enter Gentlemen Gentlemen Lawrence annotates “Lamprey and Spitchcock” (p. 61). [, who stand apart]

sp.speaker: LAMPREY
sp.p: Look you, did not I tell you he lay like the devil in chains, when he was bound for a thousand year?

sp.speaker: SPITCHCOCK
sp.p: But I think the devil had no steel bedstaffs. He goes beyond him for that.

sp.speaker: LAMPREY
sp.p: Nay, do but mark the conceit of his drinking. One must wipe his mouth for him with a muckinder. Do you see, sir?

sp.speaker: SPITCHCOCK
sp.p: Is this the sick trampler? Why, he is only bedrid with drinking.

sp.speaker: LAMPREY
sp.p: True, sir. He spies us.

sp.speaker: DAMPIT
sp.p: What, Sir Tristram? You come and see a weak man here, a very weak man.

sp.speaker: LAMPREY
sp.p: If you be weak in body, you should be strong in prayer, sir.

sp.speaker: DAMPIT
sp.p: Oh, I have pray’d too much, poor man.

sp.speaker: LAMPREY
sp.p: [To Spitchcock] There’s a taste of his soul for you.

sp.speaker: SPITCHCOCK
sp.p: [To Lamprey] Faugh! Loathsome!

sp.speaker: LAMPREY
sp.p: I come to borrow a hundred pound of you, sir.

sp.speaker: DAMPIT
sp.p: Alas, you come at an ill time. I cannot spare it, i’ faith. I ha’ but two thousand i’ th’ house.

sp.speaker: AUDREY
sp.p: Ha, ha, ha!

sp.speaker: DAMPIT
sp.p: Out, you gernative quean, the mullipood of villainy, the spinner of concupiscency!

sp.speaker: SIR LANCELOT
sp.p: Yea, gentlemen, are you here before us? How is he now?

sp.speaker: LAMPREY
sp.p: Faith, the same man still. The tavern bitch has bit him i’ th’ head.

sp.speaker: SIR LANCELOT
sp.p: We shall have the better sport with him. Peace.—And how cheers Master Dampit now?

sp.speaker: DAMPIT
sp.p: Oh, my bosom Sir Lancelot, how cheer I? Thy presence is restorative.

sp.speaker: SIR LANCELOT
sp.p: But I hear a great complaint of you, Master Dampit, among gallants.

sp.speaker: DAMPIT
sp.p: I am glad of that, i’ faith. Prithee, what?

sp.speaker: SIR LANCELOT
sp.p: They say you are wax’d proud a’ late, and if a friend visit you in the afternoon, you’ll scarce know him.

sp.speaker: DAMPIT
sp.p: Fie, fie! Proud? I cannot remember any such thing. Sure, I was drunk then.

sp.speaker: SIR LANCELOT
sp.p: Think you so, sir?

sp.speaker: DAMPIT
sp.p: There ‘twas, i’ faith. Nothing but the pride of the sack, and so certify ‘em. Fetch sack, sirrah.

p.seg: A vengeance sack you once!

sp.speaker: AUDREY
sp.p: Why, Master Dampit, if you hold on as you begin and lie a little longer, you need not take care how to dispose your wealth; you’ll make the vintner your heir.

sp.speaker: DAMPIT
sp.p: Out, you babliaminy, you unfeather’d cremitoried quean, you cullisance of scabiosity!

sp.speaker: AUDREY
sp.p: Good words, Master Dampit, to speak before a maid and a virgin!

sp.speaker: DAMPIT
sp.p: Hang thy virginity upon the pole of carnality.

sp.speaker: AUDREY
sp.p: Sweet terms! My mistress shall know ‘em.

p.seg: Note but the misery of this usuring slave. Here he lies, like a noisome dunghill, full of the poison of his drunken blasphemies, and they to whom he bequeaths all grudge him the very meat that feeds him, the very pillow that eases him. Here may a usurer behold his end. What profits it to be a slave in this world and a devil i’ th’ next?

sp.speaker: DAMPIT
sp.p: Sir Lancelot, let me buss thee, Sir Lancelot. Thou art the only friend that I honour and respect.

sp.speaker: SIR LANCELOT
sp.p: I thank you for that, Master Dampit.

sp.speaker: DAMPIT
sp.p: Farewell, my bosom Sir Lancelot.

p.seg: Gentlemen, and you love me, let me step behind you, and one of you fall a-talking of me to him.
Content.

sp.speaker: DAMPIT
sp.p: So, sir?

sp.speaker: LAMPREY
sp.p: Here came Sir Lancelot to see you e’en now.

sp.speaker: DAMPIT
sp.p: Hang him, rascal!

sp.speaker: LAMPREY
sp.p: Who, Sir Lancelot?

sp.speaker: DAMPIT
sp.p: Pythagorical rascal!

sp.speaker: LAMPREY
sp.p: Pythagorical?

sp.speaker: DAMPIT
sp.p: Ay. He changes his cloak when he meets a sergeant.

p.seg: What a rogue’s this!

sp.speaker: LAMPREY
sp.p: I wonder you can rail at him, sir; he comes in love to see you.

sp.speaker: DAMPIT
sp.p: A louse for his love! His father was a combmaker. I have no need of his crawling love. He comes to have longer day, the superlative rascal.

p.seg: ‘Sfoot, I can no longer endure the rogue.

sp.speaker: DAMPIT
sp.p: Who? My dear and kind Sir Lancelot? The only gentleman of England. Let me hug thee. Farewell, and a thousand.

p.seg: Compos’d of wrongs and slavish flatteries.
Nay, gentlemen, he shall show you more tricks yet. I’ll give you another taste of him.
Is’t possible?
His memory is upon departing.

sp.speaker: DAMPIT
sp.p: Another cup of sack!

p.seg: Mass, then ‘twill be quite gone. Before he drink that, tell him there’s a country client come up, and here attends for his learned advice.
Enough.

sp.speaker: DAMPIT
sp.p: One cup more, and then let the bell toll. I hope I shall be weak enough by that time.

sp.speaker: LAMPREY
sp.p: Master Dampit.

sp.speaker: DAMPIT
sp.p: Is the sack spouting?

sp.speaker: LAMPREY
sp.p: ‘Tis coming forward, sir. [Enter Boy with sack] Here’s a countryman, a client of yours, waits for your deep and profound advice, sir.

sp.speaker: DAMPIT
sp.p: A coxcombry? Where is he? Let him approach. Set me up a peg higher.

sp.speaker: LAMPREY
sp.p: You must draw near, sir.

sp.speaker: DAMPIT
sp.p: Now, good man fooliaminy, what say you to me now?

sp.speaker: SIR LANCELOT
sp.p: Please your good worship, I am a poor man, sir,—

sp.speaker: DAMPIT
sp.p: What make you in my chamber then?

sp.speaker: SIR LANCELOT
sp.p: I would entreat your worship’s device in a just and honest cause, sir.

sp.speaker: DAMPIT
sp.p: I meddle with no such matters. I refer ‘em to Master No-man’s office.

sp.speaker: SIR LANCELOT
sp.p: I had but one house left me in all the world, sir, which was my father’s, my grandfather’s, my great-grandfather’s, and now a villain has unjustly wrung me out and took possession on’t.

sp.speaker: DAMPIT
sp.p: Has he such feats? Thy best course is to bring thy ejectione firmae , and in seven year thou mayst shove him out by the law.

sp.speaker: SIR LANCELOT
sp.p: Alas, an’t please your worship, I have small friends and less money.

sp.speaker: DAMPIT
sp.p: Hoyday! This gear will fadge well! Hast no money? Why, then, my advice is thou must set fire a’ th’ house, and so get him out.

sp.speaker: LAMPREY
sp.p: That will break strife indeed!

p.seg: Altering but my voice a little, you see he knew me not. You may observe by this that a drunkard’s memory holds longer in the voice than in the person. But, gentlemen, shall I show you a sight? Behold the little dive-dapper of damnation, Gulf the usurer, for his time worse than tother.

sp.speaker: LAMPREY
sp.p: What’s he comes with him?

sp.speaker: SIR LANCELOT
sp.p: Why, Hoard, that married lately the widow Medlar.

sp.speaker: LAMPREY
sp.p: Oh, I cry you mercy, sir.

sp.speaker: WALKADINE HOARD
sp.p: Now, gentlemen visitants, how does Master Dampit?

sp.speaker: SIR LANCELOT
sp.p: Faith, here he lies, e’en drawing in, sir, good canary as fast as he can, sir. A very weak creature, truly. He is almost past memory.

sp.speaker: WALKADINE HOARD
sp.p: Fie, Master Dampit, you lie lazing abed here, and I come to invite you to my wedding dinner. Up, up, up!

sp.speaker: DAMPIT
sp.p: Who’s this? Master Hoard? Who hast thou married, in the name of foolery?

sp.speaker: WALKADINE HOARD
sp.p: A rich widow.

sp.speaker: DAMPIT
sp.p: A Dutch widow!

sp.speaker: WALKADINE HOARD
sp.p: A rich widow, one widow Medlar.

sp.speaker: DAMPIT
sp.p: Medlar! She keeps open house.

sp.speaker: WALKADINE HOARD
sp.p: She did, I can tell you, in her tother husband’s days, open house for all comers. Horse and man was welcome, and room enough for ‘em all.

sp.speaker: DAMPIT
sp.p: There’s too much for thee then. Thou mayst let out some to thy neighbours.

sp.speaker: GULF
sp.p:
What, hung alive in chains? Oh, spectacle! Bedstaffs of steel? O monstrum horrendum, informe, ingens cui lumen
ademptum! O Dampit, Dampit, here’s a just judgment shown upon usury, extortion, and trampling villainy.

p.seg: This [is] ex’llent, thief rails upon the thief!

sp.speaker: GULF
sp.p: Is this the end of cut-throat usury, brothel, and blasphemy? Now mayst thou see what race a usurer runs.

sp.speaker: DAMPIT
sp.p: Why, thou rogue of universality, do not I know thee? Thy sound is like the cuckoo, the Welsh ambassador. Thou cowardly slave, that offers to fight with a sick man when his weapon’s down! Rail upon me in my naked bed? Why, thou great Lucifer’s little vicar, I am not so weak but I know a knave at first sight. Thou inconscionable rascal, thou that goest upon Middlesex juries and will make haste to give up thy verdict because thou wilt not lose thy dinner, are you answered?

sp.speaker: GULF
sp.p: An’t were not for shame—

sp.speaker: DAMPIT
sp.p: Thou wouldst be hang’d then.

sp.speaker: LAMPREY
sp.p: Nay, you must exercise patience, Master Gulf, always in a sick man’s chamber.

sp.speaker: SIR LANCELOT
sp.p: [To Dampit] He’ll quarrel with none, I warrant you, but those that are bedrid.

sp.speaker: DAMPIT
sp.p: Let him come, gentlemen, I am arm’d. Reach my closestool hither.

sp.speaker: SIR LANCELOT
sp.p: Here will be a sweet fray anon. I’ll leave you, gentlemen.

sp.speaker: LAMPREY
sp.p: Nay, we’ll along with you. Master Gulf.

sp.speaker: GULF
sp.p: Hang him, usuring rascal.

sp.speaker: SIR LANCELOT
sp.p: Push! Set your strength to his, your wit to his.

sp.speaker: AUDREY
sp.p: Pray, gentlemen, depart, His hour’s come upon him.— Sleep in my bosom, sleep.

sp.speaker: SIR LANCELOT
sp.p: Nay, we have enough of him, i’ faith. Keep him for the house.

lg.l: Now make your best;
For thrice his wealth, I would not have his breast.

sp.speaker: GULF
sp.p: A little thing would make me beat him, now he’s asleep.

sp.speaker: SIR LANCELOT
sp.p: Mass, then ‘twill be a pitiful day when he wakes. I would be loath to see that day.

sp.speaker: GULF
sp.p: You overrule me, gentlemen, i’ faith.

lg.l: Nay, uncle, let me prevail with you so much.
I’ faith, go, now he has invited you.

sp.speaker: LUCRE
sp.p: I shall have great joy there when he has borne away the widow!

sp.speaker: WITGOOD
sp.p: Why, la, I thought where I should find you presently. Uncle, a’ my troth, ‘tis nothing so.

sp.speaker: LUCRE
sp.p: What’s nothing so, sir? Is not he married to the widow?

sp.speaker: WITGOOD
sp.p: No, by my troth, is he not, uncle.

sp.speaker: LUCRE
sp.p: How!

sp.speaker: WITGOOD
sp.p: Will you have the truth on’t? He is married to a whore, i’ faith.

sp.speaker: LUCRE
sp.p: I should laugh at that.

sp.speaker: WITGOOD
sp.p: Uncle, let me perish in your favour if you find it not so, and that ‘tis I that have married the honest woman.

sp.speaker: LUCRE
sp.p: Ha! I’d walk ten mile afoot to see that, i’ faith.

sp.speaker: WITGOOD
sp.p: And see’t you shall, or I’ll ne’er see you again.

sp.speaker: LUCRE
sp.p: A quean, i’ faith? Ha, ha, ha!

div2.head: [ACT V SCENE 2]
div2.stage: Enter [Walkadine] Hoard, tasting wine, the Host following in a livery cloak

sp.speaker: WALKADINE HOARD
sp.p: Pup, pup, pup, pup. I like not this wine. Is there never a better tierce in the house?

sp.speaker: HOST
sp.p: Yes, sir, there are as good tierce in the house as any are in England.

sp.speaker: WALKADINE HOARD
sp.p: Desire your mistress, you knave, to taste ‘em all over; she has better skill.

p.seg: The better for her and the worse for you.

sp.speaker: WALKADINE HOARD
sp.p: Arthur, is the cupboard of plate set out?

sp.speaker: ARTHUR
sp.p: All’s in order, sir.

sp.speaker: WALKADINE HOARD
sp.p: I am in love with my liveries every time I think on ‘em. They make a gallant show, by my troth.—Niece!

sp.speaker: NIECE
sp.p: Do you call, sir?

sp.speaker: WALKADINE HOARD
sp.p: Prithee, show a little diligence and overlook the knaves a little. They’ll filch and steal today, and send whole pasties home to their wives. And thou be’st a good niece, do not see me purloin’d.

p.seg: Though the feast be prepared for you, yet it serves fit for my wedding dinner too.

sp.speaker: WALKADINE HOARD
sp.p: Master Lamprey, and Master Spitchcock too! The most welcome gentlemen alive! Your fathers and mine were all free o’ th’ fishmongers.

sp.speaker: LAMPREY
sp.p: They were indeed, sir. You see bold guests, sir, soon entreated.

sp.speaker: WALKADINE HOARD
sp.p: And that’s best, sir. [Enter Servant] How now, sirrah?

sp.speaker: SERVANT
sp.p: There’s a coach come to th’ door, sir.

sp.speaker: WALKADINE HOARD
sp.p: My Lady Foxstone, a’ my life!—Mistress Jane Hoard! Wife!—Mass, ‘tis her ladyship indeed. [Enter Lady Foxstone] Madam, you are welcome to an unfurnish’d house, dearth of cheer, scarcity of attendance.

sp.speaker: LADY
sp.p: You are pleas’d to make the worst, sir.

sp.speaker: WALKADINE HOARD
sp.p: Wife!

sp.speaker: LADY
sp.p: Is this your bride?

sp.speaker: WALKADINE HOARD
sp.p: Yes, madam.—Salute my Lady Foxstone.

sp.speaker: COURTESAN
sp.p: Please you, madam, a while to taste the air in the garden?

sp.speaker: LADY
sp.p: ‘Twill please us well.

lg.l: Who would not wed? The most delicious life!
No joys are like the comforts of a wife.

sp.speaker: LAMPREY
sp.p: So we bachelors think, that are not troubled with them.

sp.speaker: SERVANT
sp.p: Your worship’s brother, with another ancient gentleman, are newly alighted, sir.

sp.speaker: WALKADINE HOARD
sp.p: Master Onesiphorus Hoard? Why, now our company begins to come in. [Enter Onesiphorus Hoard, Limber, and Kix] My dear and kind brother, welcome, i’ faith.

sp.speaker: ONESIPHORUS HOARD
sp.p: You see we are men at an hour, brother.

sp.speaker: WALKADINE HOARD
sp.p: Ay, I’ll say that for you, brother; you keep as good an hour to come to a feast as any gentleman in the shire.—What, old Master Limber and Master Kix! Do we meet, i’ faith, jolly gentlemen?

sp.speaker: LIMBER
sp.p: We hope you lack guests, sir.

sp.speaker: WALKADINE HOARD
sp.p: Oh, welcome, welcome! We lack still such guests as your worships.

sp.speaker: ONESIPHORUS HOARD
sp.p: Ah, sirrah brother, have you catch’d up widow Medlar?

sp.speaker: WALKADINE HOARD
sp.p: From ‘em all, brother, and, I may tell you, I had mighty enemies, those that stuck sore. Old Lucre is a sore fox, I can tell you, brother.

sp.speaker: ONESIPHORUS HOARD
sp.p: Where is she? I’ll go seek her out. I long to have a smack at her lips.

sp.speaker: WALKADINE HOARD
sp.p: And most wishfully, brother. See where she comes. [Enter Courtesan] Give her a smack now we may hear it all the house over.

sp.speaker: COURTESAN
sp.p: O Heaven, I am betray’d! I know that face.

sp.speaker: WALKADINE HOARD
sp.p: Ha, ha, ha! Why, how now? Are you both asham’d? Come, gentlemen, we’ll look another way.

sp.speaker: ONESIPHORUS HOARD
sp.p: Nay, brother, hark you. Come, y’are dispos’d to be merry.

sp.speaker: WALKADINE HOARD
sp.p: Why do we meet else, man?

sp.speaker: ONESIPHORUS HOARD
sp.p: That’s another matter. I was ne’er so ‘fraid in my life but that you had been in earnest.

sp.speaker: WALKADINE HOARD
sp.p: How mean you, brother?

sp.speaker: ONESIPHORUS HOARD
sp.p: You said she was your wife.

sp.speaker: WALKADINE HOARD
sp.p: Did I so? By my troth, and so she is.

sp.speaker: ONESIPHORUS HOARD
sp.p: By your troth, brother?

sp.speaker: WALKADINE HOARD
sp.p: What reason have I to dissemble with my friends, brother? If marriage can make her mine, she is mine. Why?

sp.speaker: ONESIPHORUS HOARD
sp.p: Troth, I am not well of a sudden. I must crave pardon, brother. I came to see you, but I cannot stay dinner, i’ faith.

sp.speaker: WALKADINE HOARD
sp.p: I hope you will not serve me so, brother.

sp.speaker: LIMBER
sp.p: By your leave, Master Hoard.

sp.speaker: WALKADINE HOARD
sp.p: What now? What now? Pray, gentlemen, you were wont to show yourselves wise men.

sp.speaker: LIMBER
sp.p: But you have shown your folly too much here.

sp.speaker: WALKADINE HOARD
sp.p: How!

lg.l: Fie, fie! A man of your repute and name!
You’ll feast your friends, but cloy ‘em first with shame.

sp.speaker: WALKADINE HOARD
sp.p: This grows too deep. Pray, let us reach the sense.

sp.speaker: LIMBER
sp.p: In your old age dote on a courtesan!

sp.speaker: WALKADINE HOARD
sp.p: Ha!

sp.speaker: KIX
sp.p: Marry a strumpet!

sp.speaker: WALKADINE HOARD
sp.p: Gentlemen!

sp.speaker: ONESIPHORUS HOARD
sp.p: And Witgood’s quean!

sp.speaker: WALKADINE HOARD
sp.p: Oh! Nor lands nor living?

lg.l: Living?
[To Courtesan] Speak!
Alas, you know at first, sir.
I told you I had nothing.

sp.speaker: WALKADINE HOARD
sp.p: Out, out! I am cheated, infinitely cozen’d!

sp.speaker: LIMBER
sp.p: Nay, Master Hoard.

sp.speaker: WALKADINE HOARD
sp.p: A Dutch widow, a Dutch widow, a Dutch widow!

lg.l: Why, nephew, shall I trace thee still a liar?
Wilt make me mad? Is not yon thing the widow?
Why, la, you are so hard a’ belief, uncle.
By my troth, she’s a whore.
Then thou’rt a knave.

sp.speaker: WITGOOD
sp.p: Negatur argumentum , uncle.

sp.speaker: LUCRE
sp.p: Probo tibi , nephew. He that knows a woman to be a quean must needs be a knave. Thou say’st thou know’st her to be one. Ergo , if she be a quean, thou’rt a knave.

sp.speaker: WITGOOD
sp.p: Negatur sequela majoris , uncle. He that knows a woman to be a quean must needs be a knave, I deny that.

sp.speaker: WALKADINE HOARD
sp.p: Lucre and Witgood, y’are both villains! Get you out of my house!

sp.speaker: LUCRE
sp.p: Why, didst not invite me to thy wedding dinner?

sp.speaker: WITGOOD
sp.p: And are not you and I sworn perpetual friends, before witness, sir, and were both drunk upon’t?

sp.speaker: WALKADINE HOARD
sp.p: Daintily abused! Y’ave put a junt upon me.

sp.speaker: LUCRE
sp.p: Ha, ha, ha!

sp.speaker: WALKADINE HOARD
sp.p: A common strumpet!

lg.l: Nay, now
You wrong her, sir. If I were she, I’d have
The law on you for that. I durst depose for her
She ne’er had common use nor common thought.
Despise me, publish me, I am your wife.
What shame can I have now but you’ll have part?
If in disgrace you share, I sought not you.
You pursued me, nay, forc’d me.
Had I friends would follow it,
Less than your action has been prov’d a rape.

sp.speaker: ONESIPHORUS HOARD
sp.p: Brother,—

sp.speaker: COURTESAN

lg.l: Nor did I ever boast of lands unto you,
Money, or goods. I took a plainer course,
And told you true I’d nothing.
If error were committed, ‘twas by you,
Thank your own folly. Nor has my sin been
So odious but worse has been forgiven.
Nor am I so deform’d but I may challenge
The utmost power of any old man’s love.

sp.p: She that tastes not sin before, twenty to one but she’ll taste it after. Most of you old men are content to marry young virgins and take that which follows; where, marrying one of us, you both save a sinner and are quit from a cuckold for ever.

lg.l: And more, in brief, let this your best thoughts win,
She that knows sin, knows best how to hate sin.
Curs’d be all malice! Black are the fruits of spite
And poison first their owners. Oh, my friends,
I must embrace shame to be rid of shame.
Conceal’d disgrace prevents a public name.
Ah, Witgood, ah, Theodorus,—

sp.speaker: WITGOOD
sp.p: Alas, sir, I was prick’d in conscience to see her well bestow’d, and where could I bestow her better than upon your pitiful worship? Excepting but myself, I dare swear she’s a virgin; and now by marrying your niece I have banish’d myself for ever from her. She’s mine aunt now, by my faith, and there’s no meddling with mine aunt, you know, a sin against my nuncle.

lg.l: Lo, gentlemen, before you all
In true reclaimed form I fall.
Henceforth for ever I defy
The glances of a sinful eye,
Waving of fans, which some suppose
Tricks of fancy, treading of toes,
Wringing of fingers, biting the lip,
The wanton gait, th’alluring trip,
All secret friends and private meetings,
Close-borne letters and bawds’ greetings,
Feigning excuse to women’s labours
When we are sent for to th’ next neighbours,
Taking false physic and ne’er start
To be let blood, though sign be at heart,
Removing chambers, shifting beds,
To welcome friends in husbands’ steads,
Them to enjoy and you to marry,
They first serv’d while you must tarry,
They to spend and you to gather,
They to get and you to father.
These and thousand thousand more,
New reclaim’d, I now abhor.
Ah, here’s a lesson, rioter, for you!
I must confess my follies. I’ll down too,
And here for ever I disclaim
The cause of youth’s undoing: Game,
Chiefly dice, those true outlanders
That shake out beggars, thieves, and panders;
Soul-wasting surfeits, sinful riots,
Queans’ evils, doctors’ diets,
‘Pothecaries’ drugs, surgeons’ glisters,
Stabbing of arms for a common mistress,
Riband favours, ribald speeches,
Dear perfum’d jackets, penniless breeches,
Dutch flapdragons, healths in urine,
Drabs that keep a man too sure in,
I do defy you all.
Lend me each honest hand, for here I rise
A reclaim’d man, loathing the general vice.
So, so, all friends. The wedding dinner cools.
Who seem most crafty prove oftimes most fools.
